Met in “Galaxies and Hubble’s law”.]] gives v = H₀d, so the time is d ÷ (H₀d) = **1 ÷ H₀**, and the distance cancels. *Every* galaxy, near or far, gives the same answer, which is why the expansion can be dated at all: all the galaxies were together at one moment, and that moment is a time 1 ÷ H₀ ago, the **expansion age** of the universe.

reveal.text: For the galaxies each has its own distance and its own speed, and Hubble’s law makes the time come out the same for all of them.

lead.text: The [[Hubble constant|The number H₀ in Hubble’s law, about 70 km/s per Mpc. Met in “Galaxies and Hubble’s law”.]] has units of km/s per Mpc, and to get a time *the distance unit has to be removed*. One Mpc is 3.086 × 10¹⁹ km, so H₀ = 60 km/s per Mpc means 60 km/s for every 3.086 × 10¹⁹ km, and the kilometres cancel in 1 ÷ H₀ = 3.086 × 10¹⁹ km ÷ 60 km/s = 5.14 × 10¹⁷ s. That is in seconds, and one billion years is 3.156 × 10¹⁶ s, so dividing gives 16.3 billion years.
Doing the conversion once for every value of H₀ gives a constant, since 3.086 × 10¹⁹ ÷ 3.156 × 10¹⁶ = 977.8, and so **1 ÷ H₀ = 977.8 billion years ÷ H₀**, with H₀ in km/s per Mpc.

reveal.text: That is close to the accepted age of the universe, and the next screen compares the two.

lead.text: For H₀ = 70 km/s per Mpc the expansion age 977.8 ÷ 70 is about 14 billion years, and the accepted age of the universe is 13.8 billion years. The two nearly agree, but they ought not to agree exactly, because 1 ÷ H₀ assumes that every galaxy has moved at its present speed throughout, and the expansion has not been steady.

Gravity slowed the expansion in the first several billion years, which makes the true age *shorter* than 1 ÷ H₀. In 1998 two teams of astronomers found from distant supernovae that the expansion has been speeding up for about the last six billion years, a change attributed to **dark energy**, the name given to whatever drives it, and that makes the true age *longer*. The two effects nearly cancel, so 1 ÷ H₀ happens to land close to 13.8 billion years.
A smaller Hubble constant means a slower expansion.

reveal.text: A slower expansion needs longer to spread the galaxies out to their present distances, which is why the age rises as H₀ falls.

lead.text: Run the expansion back far enough and the universe was smaller and also hotter, since squeezing a gas heats it. When it was about 380,000 years old it was a glowing gas at about 3,000 K, so opaque that light could not travel far. As the expansion cooled the gas below that temperature, electrons and nuclei combined into atoms, the gas became transparent, and the light that had been trapped streamed away in every direction.

That light is still travelling, and it reaches us from *every* direction as the **cosmic microwave background**. Its wavelengths have been stretched as space expanded, so the glow that began at 3,000 K now has the spectrum of a [[blackbody|An ideal glowing body whose spectrum depends only on its temperature. Met in “Temperature, colour and motion”.]] at 2.725 K, whose peak, by [[Wien’s law|The peak wavelength is 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K divided by the temperature in kelvin. Met in “Temperature, colour and motion”.]], lies in the microwave region.

afterFigure.text: Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson found the glow by accident in 1965, as a steady hiss in a radio antenna at Bell Laboratories that no direction of the sky could remove.

reveal.text: A peak of about a millimetre lies in the microwave region, between the infrared and the radio waves, which gives the glow its name.

lead.text: While the light has crossed the expanding universe, its wavelengths have been stretched in the same proportion as space. By [[Wien’s law|The peak wavelength is 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K divided by the temperature in kelvin. Met in “Temperature, colour and motion”.]] the peak wavelength is inversely proportional to the temperature, so a stretch of the wavelengths by any factor lowers the temperature of the glow by *that same factor*.

A glow at 300 K, about the temperature of a room, peaks near 10 µm in the infrared, and stretched 100 times its peak moves to about 1 mm and its temperature falls to 3 K. **The factor by which the background has been stretched since its release is therefore the earlier temperature divided by the temperature now.**

cases.label: The same glow stretched 100 times, 3 K

reveal.text: A stretch by a factor of about a thousand takes light from the visible and infrared ranges into the microwave range.

lessons.orientation: How 1 ÷ H₀ estimates the age of the universe, and how the cosmic microwave background is the stretched afterglow of its hot early state.
lessons.reviewLabel: The age and afterglow of the Big Bang
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Play the expansion **backwards** and every galaxy moves back towards us, and because the farther galaxies move faster in exactly the proportion that they are farther, they all return at the same moment, whatever their distance. That moment is the beginning of the expansion, which is what the name Big Bang describes.
The moment can be dated from H₀ alone, since the time taken to cover a distance at a steady speed is the distance divided by the speed.

intro.promise: By the end you’ll be able to estimate the age of the universe from H₀ and read the temperature and stretch of the microwave glow.

recap.keyIdea: Running the expansion backwards gives an age of 1 ÷ H₀, about 14 billion years for H₀ = 70 km/s per Mpc and close to the accepted 13.8 billion, and the microwave background is the stretched afterglow of the hot early universe.

blocks.text: Because every galaxy’s speed is proportional to its distance, all of them were together a time 1 ÷ H₀ ago, which is 977.8 billion years ÷ H₀ with H₀ in km/s per Mpc. The true age is 13.8 billion years, because gravity slowed the expansion early on and dark energy has sped it up since, and the two effects nearly cancel.

The universe was a glowing gas of about 3,000 K when it became transparent, and the light of that glow has been stretched by a factor of about 1,100, so that its blackbody spectrum now peaks near a millimetre at 2.725 K, as the [[cosmic microwave background|The faint microwave glow from all directions, left over from when the universe became transparent. Met in “The age and afterglow of the Big Bang”.]].

questions.prompt: Cairo is at latitude 30° N. Roughly how high above the northern horizon does the north celestial pole stand there?
hints: At the equator the pole sits on the horizon, and at the North Pole it is overhead. Think about how far along that range Cairo’s latitude lies.
Compare the pole's height at the equator and at the North Pole with the latitude at each place, and look for the rule that fits both.
questions.onCorrect: The pole stands about 30° above the horizon, the same as the latitude, and the next screen shows that this holds at every latitude.

misconceptions.feedback: 60° is 90° minus the latitude, which is the angle from the pole up to the zenith. The height asked for is measured up from the horizon.
90° is the pole’s height at the North Pole, where the latitude is 90°. Cairo lies much nearer to the equator.

questions.prompt: The sky turns steadily, making one full turn in about 24 hours, which is 15° an hour. About what part of a full turn does a star move through in 6 hours?
hints: How many hours does a full turn of the sky take, and how many of those hours have passed?
The sky turns steadily, so equal times give equal angles. What fraction of the day is 6 hours?

acceptedIdeas: A quarter of a full turn
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A quarter of a full turn

choices.label: A sixth of a full turn
A quarter of a full turn

questions.onCorrect: A full turn takes 24 hours, and 6 hours is a quarter of that. Because the sky turns steadily, a quarter of the time gives a quarter of the angle, which is 90°.

misconceptions.feedback: That reads the 6 hours as six equal parts of a turn. A full turn takes 24 hours, so 6 hours is 6 parts out of 24, which is a larger share than a sixth.
Half a turn takes 12 hours, and a full turn takes 24, so 6 hours is a smaller share of a turn than a half.

questions.prompt: From Amsterdam, at latitude 52° N, every star north of declination +38° never sets. Suppose you travel north to latitude 60° N. What happens to that limit?
hints: How high does the north celestial pole stand at 60° N compared with 52° N?
A star never sets when its whole circle stays above the horizon. Does a higher pole make that easier or harder?

acceptedIdeas: It moves south of +38°, so more stars never set
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It moves south of +38°, so more stars never set

choices.label: It moves north of +38°, so fewer stars never set
It moves south of +38°, so more stars never set
It stays at +38°, since declinations are fixed

questions.onCorrect: The limit is 90° minus the latitude, so it falls from 38° to 30° as you move north. A higher pole lifts the whole circle of every star, so stars nearer the celestial equator now stay above the horizon all night.

misconceptions.feedback: That reverses the effect of latitude. The limit is 90° minus the latitude, so work out which way it moves when the latitude rises.
A star’s declination does stay fixed, but the limit does not. It depends on your latitude, which sets how high the pole stands, and so how large a circle can stay above the horizon.

questions.prompt: From latitude 52° N, one star of declination +20° and another of declination +50° cross the meridian. The zenith at 52° N lies at declination +52°. Which star climbs higher?
hints: At which declination does the zenith lie, and which star’s declination is closer to it?
A star crosses the meridian at its highest point of the night. How far below the zenith does each of these two stars cross?

acceptedIdeas: The +50° star, which passes near the zenith
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The +50° star, which passes near the zenith

choices.label: The +20° star, which lies nearer the celestial equator
Both climb equally high, since both lie north of the equator
The +50° star, which passes near the zenith

questions.onCorrect: A star’s height on the meridian is 90° minus its distance from the zenith. The +50° star lies only 2° from the zenith, while the +20° star lies 32° from it, so the +50° star crosses much higher.

misconceptions.feedback: Nearness to the celestial equator does not set the height. A star climbs highest when its declination matches your latitude, because it then crosses the meridian at the zenith.
Stars at different declinations cross the meridian at different heights. Each height is set by how far the star lies from the zenith, which here is at +52°.

questions.prompt: From latitude 30° N, one star of declination +10° and another of declination −10° cross the meridian. Which climbs higher?
hints: At latitude 30° N, at which declination does the zenith lie?
How far from that declination is each of the two stars, with the minus sign counted?

acceptedIdeas: The +10° star, which lies nearer the zenith
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The +10° star, which lies nearer the zenith

choices.label: The +10° star, which lies nearer the zenith
Both reach the same height, since each is 10° from the equator
It depends on the time of night at which you look

questions.onCorrect: The zenith at 30° N lies at declination +30°. The +10° star is 20° from it and the −10° star is 40° from it, so the +10° star crosses the meridian higher, at 70° against 50°.

misconceptions.feedback: Each star is 10° from the celestial equator, but on opposite sides of it, and the zenith at 30° N lies north of the equator. A southern declination keeps its minus sign, and that changes how far the star lies from the zenith.

Each star’s highest point comes when it crosses the meridian, and that height is fixed by its declination and your latitude. The two stars cross at different times, but the time of night does not change the height of either crossing.

questions.prompt: What single word names a star that never sets as seen from a given latitude?
hints: The star's circle stays around the pole without dipping below the horizon.
Ask where a star's lowest point falls as the sky turns, and which stars never reach the horizon.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Circumpolar: its whole daily circle stays above the horizon around the celestial pole.

questions.onCorrect: Circumpolar: the whole daily circle stays above the horizon.

misconceptions.feedback: The meridian is a line across the sky, not a kind of star. The word you want describes a star that never sets.

questions.prompt: London is at latitude 51.5° N, and Earth’s axis is tilted by 23.4°. At the June solstice, how does London’s noon Sun compare in height with the noon Sun at an equinox?
hints: What is the Sun’s declination at an equinox, and what is it at the June solstice?
The noon altitude is 90° minus the gap between your latitude and the Sun’s declination. What happens to that gap as the declination rises towards your latitude?

acceptedIdeas: About 23° higher, a rise equal to the tilt
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 23° higher, a rise equal to the tilt

choices.label: About 47° higher, a rise equal to twice the tilt
About 23° higher, a rise equal to the tilt
No higher, since noon height depends only on latitude

questions.onCorrect: The Sun’s declination rises from 0° at an equinox to +23.4° at the June solstice, and London lies north of both, so the gap to its latitude shrinks by 23.4°. The noon Sun therefore stands 23.4° higher, at 61.9° instead of 38.5°.

misconceptions.feedback: Twice the tilt is the difference between the June and December Sun, since the declination swings from +23.4° to −23.4°. Count how far the declination moves between an equinox and June.
The noon height depends on the Sun’s declination as well as on the latitude. The declination grows from 0° at an equinox to +23.4° in June, which brings the noon Sun nearer the zenith.

questions.prompt: London’s noon Sun stands about 62° high at the June solstice and about 38° high at an equinox. Taking Earth’s tilt as 23.4°, which is the best estimate of its height at the December solstice?
hints: Which way does the Sun’s declination move between an equinox and the December solstice?
London lies north of the Sun at every date. Does a lower declination bring the Sun nearer to London’s zenith, or farther from it?
questions.onCorrect: At the December solstice the declination is −23.4°, so the gap to London’s latitude grows to 74.9° and the noon Sun stands 90° − 74.9° = 15.1° high. That is the equinox height lowered by one tilt, where June raises it by one tilt.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the June height. In December the Sun’s declination is negative, which puts the Sun farther from London’s latitude, so the noon height cannot match June’s.
That is the equinox height, which holds only when the declination is 0°. In December the declination is −23.4°, which lowers the noon Sun below it.

questions.prompt: At an equinox the Sun’s declination is 0°, wherever you stand. How does the noon Sun’s height at 40° N compare with its height at 60° N?
hints: At an equinox, how far is the Sun from your zenith when you stand at latitude φ?
Which of the two places lies farther from the equator, and what does that do to the gap?

choices.label: The same at both, since the declination is 0°

questions.onCorrect: At an equinox the noon Sun stands 90° − φ high, so it falls one degree for every degree you travel north. That puts it at 50° over 40° N and at 30° over 60° N, a difference of 20°.

misconceptions.feedback: Going north takes you away from the celestial equator, where the Sun lies at an equinox, so the noon Sun sinks. At an equinox its height is 90° minus the latitude.
The declination is the same, but the latitude is not. The noon height is 90° minus the gap between latitude and declination, and the gap is 40° at one place and 60° at the other.

questions.prompt: Imagine that Earth had no axial tilt, so that the Sun never left the celestial equator. How would London’s noon Sun in June compare with its noon Sun in December?
hints: Without a tilt, what is the Sun’s declination on every date?
What sets the Sun’s noon height: its distance, or its declination and your latitude?

acceptedIdeas: The same height on both dates
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The same height on both dates

choices.label: The same height on both dates
Higher in June, since Earth is nearer the Sun in summer
Higher in December, since Earth is nearer the Sun in January

questions.onCorrect: The Sun’s noon height depends on its declination and your latitude, and without a tilt the declination stays at 0° on every date. London’s noon Sun would then stand at 90° − 51.5° = 38.5° all year.

misconceptions.feedback: Earth is not nearer the Sun in northern summer, and distance would not change the Sun’s height in the sky in any case. That height depends on the Sun’s declination.
Earth is nearest the Sun in January, but the distance changes by only about 3%, and it has no effect on the Sun’s height in the sky. That is set by the declination, which stays at 0° without a tilt.

questions.prompt: At the June solstice the noon Sun is directly overhead at one line of latitude. Which line is it?
hints: Directly overhead means an altitude of 90°.
Set 90° − |φ − δ| equal to 90°.
The latitude must match the Sun’s declination on that date.

acceptedIdeas: The Tropic of Cancer, at 23.4° N
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The Tropic of Cancer, at 23.4° N

choices.label: The Tropic of Cancer, at 23.4° N
The Tropic of Capricorn, at 23.4° S

questions.onCorrect: The Sun is overhead where latitude equals declination, which at the June solstice is 23.4° N, the Tropic of Cancer.

misconceptions.feedback: The overhead Sun is on the equator at the equinoxes. At the June solstice the Sun’s declination is +23.4°, so the overhead point has moved off the equator.
That is where the Sun is overhead at the December solstice, when its declination is −23.4°. At the June solstice the Sun is on the other side of the celestial equator.
66.6° is 90° minus the tilt. The Sun is overhead where the latitude equals its declination, and the Sun never reaches a declination as large as 66.6°.

questions.prompt: Why is it winter in the northern hemisphere in January?
hints: Compare the two hemispheres: they have opposite seasons at the same distance from the Sun.
Think about how the tilt changes the Sun's height at noon and the length of the day in each hemisphere.

acceptedIdeas: The northern hemisphere tilts away from the Sun, giving low noon sunlight and short days
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The northern hemisphere tilts away from the Sun, giving low noon sunlight and short days

choices.label: Earth is farthest from the Sun in January, so less sunlight reaches the whole planet
The Sun gives out less energy in January, so less sunlight reaches the whole planet
The northern hemisphere tilts away from the Sun, giving low noon sunlight and short days

questions.onCorrect: Seasons follow the tilt. In January the north leans away from the Sun, so noon sunlight is low and the days are short, even though Earth is then at its closest to the Sun.

misconceptions.feedback: Earth is nearest the Sun in early January and farthest in early July. If distance caused winter, the southern hemisphere would have winter at the same time.
The Sun’s output hardly changes through the year, and if it did both hemispheres would cool together, whereas the seasons are opposite in the north and the south.

questions.prompt: At first quarter the Sun–Earth–Moon angle is 90°. How much of the Moon’s visible disc is lit?
hints: At new moon none of the visible disc is lit, and at full moon all of it is. Where does 90° lie between them?
Picture the Moon a week after new moon. What shape is the lit part?
questions.onCorrect: At 90° the Moon is a quarter of the way round its cycle and half of the visible disc is lit, which the formula on the next screen confirms: (1 − cos 90°) ÷ 2 = 0.5.

misconceptions.feedback: “Quarter” names how far round its cycle the Moon has travelled, and not the share of the disc that is lit.
Three quarters of the disc is lit at 120°, farther round the cycle. The angle here is only 90°.

questions.prompt: The Moon gains one full turn of 360° on the Sun in a synodic month of 29.53 days. About how many degrees does it gain each day?
hints: How many degrees does the Moon gain in one synodic month, and over how many days is that gain spread?
If the gain is spread evenly, what do you do with the 360° and the number of days?
questions.onCorrect: A full turn of 360° shared over about 30 days is about 12° a day, and with the exact month of 29.53 days it comes to 12.2°. That steady gain is the rate at which the Sun–Earth–Moon angle grows.

misconceptions.feedback: That is close to how far the Sun appears to move against the stars each day, 360° in a year. The Moon gains 360° in a month, so it gains far more each day.
That reads the 29.53 days as a number of degrees. The 360° is shared out over those days, so each day gets about a thirtieth of it.

questions.prompt: At which phase of the Moon can a lunar eclipse happen? Answer with one word.
hints: Earth’s shadow points directly away from the Sun.
Earth's shadow falls on the side facing away from the Sun, so ask where the Moon must be to enter it.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Full: Earth must sit between the Sun and the Moon so the Moon can pass through Earth's shadow.

questions.onCorrect: At full moon Earth lies between the Sun and the Moon, so the Moon can pass through Earth’s shadow.

misconceptions.feedback: At new moon the Moon is between Earth and the Sun, while Earth’s shadow points away from the Sun and lies on the far side of Earth.

questions.prompt: The Sun is about 400 times as wide as the Moon and about 390 times as far away. How does the Sun’s angular diameter in our sky compare with the Moon’s?
hints: Angular size is the diameter divided by the distance. What happens to that ratio when both are about 400 times as large?
Which of the two changes is larger, and by how much?

acceptedIdeas: About the same, since the two ratios nearly cancel
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About the same, since the two ratios nearly cancel

choices.label: About 400 times larger, since it is 400 times as wide
About 390 times smaller, since it is 390 times as far
About the same, since the two ratios nearly cancel

questions.onCorrect: Angular size is the diameter divided by the distance, so a body about 400 times as wide and 390 times as far away looks almost the same size: the Moon’s 0.52° against the Sun’s 0.53°.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the width alone. Angular size is the width divided by the distance, so the Sun’s greater distance has to be set against its greater width.
That counts the distance alone. The Sun’s greater width has to be set against it.

questions.prompt: A synodic month, from one new moon to the next, lasts 29.53 days. About how long after new moon does the Moon reach first quarter?
hints: What fraction of the cycle is a quarter?
About how many weeks does a month hold, and how many of them make up that fraction?
questions.onCorrect: First quarter is a quarter of the way round the cycle, and a quarter of 29.53 days is about 7.4 days, a little over a week.

misconceptions.feedback: That is full moon, halfway round the cycle. First quarter is a quarter of the way round, so it comes sooner.
That is the third quarter, three quarters of the way round. First quarter comes before full moon, not after it.

questions.prompt: The Sun–Earth–Moon angle is 120°, which lies between first quarter at 90° and full moon at 180°. Which description of the Moon fits?
hints: Half the disc is lit at 90° and all of it at 180°. Where does 120° lie between them?
When the angle passes 90°, do we see more or less of the lit half of the Moon?

acceptedIdeas: A gibbous Moon, with more than half the disc lit
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A gibbous Moon, with more than half the disc lit

choices.label: A crescent Moon, with less than half the disc lit
A quarter Moon, with exactly half the disc lit
A gibbous Moon, with more than half the disc lit

questions.onCorrect: At 120° the cosine is −0.5, so (1 + 0.5) ÷ 2 = 0.75 and three quarters of the disc is lit. Beyond 90° we see more of the lit half than the dark half, which makes the Moon gibbous.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats cos 120° as +0.5, which would give 25%. For an angle above 90° the cosine is negative, which changes the result.
Half of the disc is lit only at 90°, and the angle here is larger than that.

questions.prompt: An asteroid’s orbit has semi-major axis 2 AU and eccentricity 0.6, so the Sun sits well off the centre of a long ellipse. About how close does the asteroid come to the Sun?
hints: How far from the centre of the ellipse does the Sun sit, as a share of a?
The near end of the orbit lies a from the centre, with the Sun a × e from the centre towards it. How far is the Sun from that near end?

choices.label: About 1.2 AU, just outside Earth’s orbit
About 2 AU, the semi-major axis itself
About 3.2 AU, beyond the semi-major axis

questions.onCorrect: Perihelion is a(1 − e) = 2 × (1 − 0.6) = 0.8 AU. An eccentricity of 0.6 takes the Sun 60% of the way from the centre towards the near end, so the asteroid comes much closer than its semi-major axis suggests.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a × e, the distance from the centre of the ellipse to the Sun. The closest approach falls short of a by that much, so it is a − a × e.
The semi-major axis is the average of the nearest and farthest distances. With an eccentricity of 0.6 the asteroid comes much closer than its average.
That is the far end of the orbit, a(1 + e). The closest point lies on the near side of the Sun.

questions.prompt: An asteroid is 1 AU from the Sun at its closest point and 4 AU at its farthest. How does its speed at the closest point compare with its speed at the farthest?
hints: Which end of the orbit has the shorter line to the Sun, and what must the asteroid do there to sweep the same area?
At the two ends, speed × distance from the Sun is the same. What does that make the ratio of the speeds?
questions.onCorrect: Equal areas in equal times make speed × distance from the Sun the same at both ends, so the speeds are in the inverse ratio of the distances: 4 AU ÷ 1 AU = 4.

misconceptions.feedback: That has the ratio upside down. The line to the Sun is shortest at the closest point, so the asteroid must move fastest there.
That squares the ratio of the distances, as for a force. Equal areas in equal times make the speeds inversely proportional to the distances, with no square.

questions.prompt: An asteroid orbits the Sun at 4 AU, four times Earth’s distance. Using P² = a³ (P in years, a in AU), how does its period compare with Earth’s year?
hints: Cube the distance first. What does that give for P²?
The period is the square root of P². Is the result larger or smaller than the distance, 4?
questions.onCorrect: P² = 4³ = 64, so P = 8 years, eight times Earth’s year. The period grows faster than the distance because the law squares P and cubes a.

misconceptions.feedback: That makes the period proportional to the distance. In Kepler’s law P² goes with a³, so the period grows faster than the distance.
That is 4², and the law has a³ on one side and P² on the other. Cube the distance first, then take the square root.

questions.prompt: A planet orbits a star of 4 solar masses at a distance of 1 AU. Using P² = a³ ÷ M, how does its period compare with Earth’s year?
hints: Does a more massive star lengthen or shorten the period at the same distance?
With a = 1 and M = 4, what does P² come to, and what is the period itself?
questions.onCorrect: P² = 1³ ÷ 4 = 0.25, so P = 0.5 years, half of Earth’s year.

misconceptions.feedback: That is P², and the period is its square root.
The star’s mass matters. A heavier star pulls harder, which makes a planet at the same distance go round faster.
A heavier star pulls harder, so the planet moves faster and its year is shorter, not longer.

questions.prompt: Jupiter takes about 12 years to go round the Sun. Using P² = a³ (P in years, a in AU), about how far from the Sun is its orbit?
hints: Square the period first. What does that give for a³?
Which whole number, cubed, comes nearest to that value?
questions.onCorrect: P² = 12² = 144 is a³, and 5³ = 125 while 6³ = 216, so a is a little over 5 AU. For Jupiter’s exact period of 11.86 years the answer is 5.2 AU.

misconceptions.feedback: That takes the number of years as the number of AU. In P² = a³ the two are not equal: for an orbit larger than 1 AU the period in years is larger than the distance in AU.
That is the square root of the period. Since P² = a³, a is the cube root of P², and not the square root of P.
That is a³, since 12² is about 144. The distance a is the cube root of that.

questions.prompt: What name is given to the point of a planet’s orbit closest to the Sun?
hints: The name is built from Greek, like the names of other points on an orbit.
It is paired with a name for the farthest point, aphelion, and both names refer to the Sun.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Perihelion, from Greek peri (near) and helios (Sun). The farthest point is aphelion.

questions.onCorrect: Perihelion comes from the Greek peri, near, and helios, the Sun, and the farthest point is aphelion.

misconceptions.feedback: Aphelion is the farthest point. The closest point has the prefix that means near.

questions.prompt: Two bodies are moved from separation r to 3r. What happens to the gravitational force between them?
hints: Compare the two falls in the opener, 4.9 m for the apple and 1.4 mm for the Moon, a ratio of about 3,600, while the Moon is about 60 times as far from Earth’s centre.
Ask what has to be done to 60 to give 3,600, and do the same to 3.

acceptedIdeas: It falls to a ninth of its value
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It falls to a ninth of its value

choices.label: It falls to a third of its value
It falls to a ninth of its value

questions.onCorrect: Tripling the separation divides the force by 3² = 9, because the pull weakens with the square of the distance, as the next screen shows.

misconceptions.feedback: A third would mean the force falls in proportion to the distance, whereas it falls with the square of the distance, so tripling the separation divides it by 9.
Moving the bodies apart weakens the pull between them, so the force falls rather than grows.

questions.prompt: At a fixed separation, one mass is doubled and the other is tripled. How does the gravitational force between them change?
hints: The force is proportional to the product of the two masses. What happens to a product when one factor doubles?
If doubling one mass doubles the force, what does tripling the other mass do to that?

acceptedIdeas: It becomes six times as strong
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It becomes six times as strong

choices.label: It becomes five times as strong
It becomes six times as strong
It becomes three times as strong

questions.onCorrect: Force is proportional to the product of the masses, so the factors multiply: 2 × 3 = 6.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the factors, 2 + 3. The force is proportional to the product of the two masses, so the factors multiply.
The larger change does not decide the result alone. Both masses appear in the product, so each change multiplies the force.

questions.prompt: Earth’s GM is 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s² and its radius is 6,371 km. Surface gravity is g = GM ÷ R². Which is about the right size for g, in m/s²?
hints: The formula needs R in metres. What is 6,371 km in metres, to the nearest power of ten?
With R about 6 × 10⁶ m, roughly how big is R², and how many times does it go into 4 × 10¹⁴?
questions.onCorrect: With R in metres, 6.371 × 10⁶ m, R² is about 4 × 10¹³ m², and 3.986 × 10¹⁴ divided by that is about 10 m/s². The exact value is 9.82 m/s².

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the radius in kilometres. GM is in m³/s², so R must be in metres. A radius a thousand times too small makes g a million times too large.
That divides by R and not by R². The field falls with the square of the distance, so the radius is squared.

questions.prompt: Earth is about 81 times as massive as the Moon. How does Earth’s pull on the Moon compare with the Moon’s pull on Earth?
hints: Think of the pair as a tug of war between two bodies.
Whatever force acts on one body from the other, the other feels a force from it.
Newton’s third law pairs the two forces.

acceptedIdeas: The two pulls are equal in size
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The two pulls are equal in size

choices.label: Earth’s pull is about 9 times as large
The two pulls are equal in size
Earth’s pull is about 81 times as large

questions.onCorrect: The two forces are an equal and opposite pair, since GMm ÷ r² is the same whichever body is called M.

misconceptions.feedback: The factor of 81 belongs to the masses. It shows up in how much each body accelerates, but the question asks about the pull itself, which is GMm ÷ r² whichever body is called M.
Nothing in the law of gravitation takes the square root of the mass ratio. The force uses the product of the two masses, which is the same number whichever body you start from.

questions.prompt: Mars has about a tenth of Earth’s GM and about half of Earth’s radius. How does its surface gravity compare with Earth’s?
hints: What does a tenth of the GM do to g?
What does half the radius do to g, remembering that R is squared?
questions.onCorrect: Surface gravity goes as GM ÷ R². A tenth of the GM divides g by 10, and half the radius multiplies it by 2² = 4, so g is 0.4 of Earth’s. The actual figures are 3.73 and 9.82 m/s².

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by the radius ratio, 0.5, and not by its square. Since g = GM ÷ R², halving R makes g four times larger and not twice.
That multiplies the two ratios. A smaller radius raises g, so the radius ratio divides and does not multiply.

questions.prompt: Why do a hammer and a feather dropped together on the Moon land together?
hints: Divide the gravitational force by the falling object’s own mass.
Newton's second law links a force to the acceleration it gives an object of mass m.

acceptedIdeas: The pull on each object is proportional to its mass, so both accelerate at GM ÷ r²
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The pull on each object is proportional to its mass, so both accelerate at GM ÷ r²

choices.label: The pull on each object is proportional to its mass, so both accelerate at GM ÷ r²
Heavier objects are pulled less per kilogram, which cancels their extra weight
The Moon’s gravity is too weak to act on light objects such as a feather

questions.onCorrect: Dividing the pull GMm ÷ r² by the object’s mass m leaves GM ÷ r², which is the same for any object.

misconceptions.feedback: The pull per kilogram does not drop for heavier objects. Check what dividing the pull GMm ÷ r² by the object’s own mass m leaves.
Gravity acts on light and heavy objects alike. The question is how the pull on each compares with its mass.

questions.prompt: Circular speed falls as the square root of the distance from Earth’s centre. Just above the surface, 6,371 km from the centre, it is about 7.9 km/s. The International Space Station orbits 6,771 km from the centre. How does its speed compare?
hints: Does a higher orbit move faster or slower than a lower one?
The distance has grown by about 6%. What does a square root do to a small percentage change?

choices.label: Slower in proportion to the distance, about 7.4 km/s

questions.onCorrect: Circular speed goes as 1 ÷ √r, so a distance about 6% larger lowers the speed by about 3%, from 7.9 km/s to about 7.7 km/s. Higher orbits are slower, but because of the square root the change is small.

misconceptions.feedback: The field is weaker farther out, so ask whether more or less sideways speed is needed there to keep missing the ground.
That makes the speed fall in proportion to the distance. Circular speed depends on the square root of the distance, so the change is smaller than that.

questions.prompt: Circular speed just above Earth’s surface is about 7.9 km/s. About how fast must a spacecraft travel from the surface to escape Earth’s gravity?
hints: Is a body in a circular orbit free of the planet, or still bound to it?
How does the formula for escape speed differ from the formula for circular speed?
questions.onCorrect: Escape speed is √(2GM ÷ r), which is √2 times the circular speed at the same distance, and 7.9 × 1.414 is about 11 km/s. The factor √2 comes from the 2 under the root.

misconceptions.feedback: That doubles the speed. The 2 in √(2GM ÷ r) sits under the square root, so it does not double the result.
That is the circular speed, at which a body stays bound to the planet. Escaping needs more: enough speed to climb out of the field entirely.

questions.prompt: Earth’s orbital speed follows from v = √(GM ÷ r), with GM☉ = 1.327 × 10²⁰ m³/s² for the Sun and r = 1.496 × 10¹¹ m. Which is about the right size for the answer?
hints: About how big is GM ÷ r in powers of ten, with the Sun’s GM and Earth’s distance in metres?
The square root halves the power of ten, and the result is in metres per second. What is that in km/s?
questions.onCorrect: GM ÷ r is about 8.9 × 10⁸ m²/s², and its square root is about 3 × 10⁴ m/s, which is 30 km/s. The exact value is 29.8 km/s.

misconceptions.feedback: That is ten times too large. GM ÷ r is about 9 × 10⁸, and taking a square root halves the power of ten.
That reads a speed in metres per second as if it were in kilometres per second. The square root gives m/s, so divide by 1,000.

questions.prompt: Tidal stretching falls as the cube of the distance. If the Moon were at half its present distance, how would its tides change?
hints: Halving the distance multiplies 1 ÷ d³ by what factor?
Is a tide a pull, or a difference between two pulls?
questions.onCorrect: A tide is a difference in pull, which scales as 1 ÷ d³, so half the distance gives 2³ = 8 times the tide.

misconceptions.feedback: That squares the factor, as for the pull itself. A tide is a difference in pull across Earth, which falls faster with distance, as 1 ÷ d³.
That follows 1 ÷ d. The difference in pull falls faster than that, as 1 ÷ d³.

questions.prompt: The Moon’s GM is about 1/80 of Earth’s, and its radius is about 1/4 of Earth’s. Escape speed is √(2GM ÷ R). How does the Moon’s escape speed compare with Earth’s 11 km/s?
hints: Escape speed goes as √(GM ÷ R). What does the Moon’s GM ÷ R come to as a fraction of Earth’s?
Is that fraction nearer 1/16 or 1/25, and which square roots do those suggest?
questions.onCorrect: The Moon’s GM ÷ R is (1/80) ÷ (1/4) = 1/20 of Earth’s, and the square root of 1/20 is about 0.22, so its escape speed is about a fifth of 11 km/s. The exact value is 2.38 km/s.

misconceptions.feedback: That takes the square root of the GM ratio and leaves out the radius. A smaller radius raises the escape speed, since it puts the surface closer to the centre.
That uses the GM ratio directly. Escape speed goes as the square root of GM ÷ R, so the ratios are combined first and the square root is taken after.

questions.prompt: Why are the tides largest around new moon and full moon?
hints: Think about where the Sun lies relative to the Earth–Moon line at those phases.
At new moon and full moon, ask whether the Sun's tidal stretch lies along the same line as the Moon's or across it.

acceptedIdeas: The Sun, Earth and Moon lie in line, so the Sun’s tidal stretch adds to the Moon’s
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The Sun, Earth and Moon lie in line, so the Sun’s tidal stretch adds to the Moon’s

choices.label: The Moon is closest to Earth at those phases, so its pull is strongest
The Sun, Earth and Moon lie in line, so the Sun’s tidal stretch adds to the Moon’s
Earth is closest to the Sun at those phases, so the Sun’s pull is strongest

questions.onCorrect: At new and full moon the Sun, Earth and Moon are in line, so the Sun’s tidal stretch adds to the Moon’s.

misconceptions.feedback: The Moon’s distance varies over the month, but not in step with its phase. Look at where the Sun lies at new and full moon.
Earth’s distance from the Sun changes through the year and not with the Moon’s phase. Look at where the Sun lies relative to the Moon at new and full moon.

questions.prompt: A probe moves from 1 AU to 2 AU from the Sun. How does the solar flux it receives change?
hints: Light spreads over a sphere of area 4πd². By what factor does that area grow when d doubles?
If the same light covers a larger area, does each square metre receive more or less of it?
questions.onCorrect: Flux follows 1 ÷ d², so doubling the distance divides it by four.

misconceptions.feedback: That halves the flux. It follows the inverse square, so the factor of 2 in the distance is squared.
That makes the flux grow. It weakens as the probe moves farther from the Sun.

questions.prompt: The Sun’s luminosity is 3.83 × 10²⁶ W. At 1 AU, which is about 1.50 × 10¹¹ m, its light has spread over a sphere. About how much power falls on each square metre facing the Sun?
hints: What is the area of a sphere of radius d, and about how large is d² here?
About how many times does that area go into the Sun’s power?
questions.onCorrect: The flux is L ÷ (4πd²). Here 4πd² is about 12.6 × 2.25 × 10²², or 2.8 × 10²³ m², and 3.83 × 10²⁶ divided by that is about 1,400 W/m². The exact value, with 1.496 × 10¹¹ m, is 1,361 W/m².

misconceptions.feedback: That uses πd², the area of a circle of radius d, and not the surface of a sphere. The sphere’s area is 4πd², four times larger.
That leaves out the 4π. The light has spread over the whole sphere, whose area is 4πd², and 4π is about 12.

questions.prompt: Proxima Centauri’s parallax is 0.768 arcseconds, a little under one arcsecond. About how far away is it, in parsecs?
hints: How is the distance in parsecs related to the parallax in arcseconds?
A star at 1 parsec has a parallax of exactly 1 arcsecond. Is this star nearer or farther than that?
questions.onCorrect: The distance in parsecs is 1 ÷ p, and 1 ÷ 0.768 is about 1.3, so Proxima lies about 1.3 pc away, which is 4.25 light-years. A parallax below 1 arcsecond always means a distance above 1 parsec.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the parallax itself. The distance in parsecs is its reciprocal, 1 ÷ p, so a parallax below 1 arcsecond means a distance above 1 parsec.
That divides by a parallax of 0.0768. The parallax is 0.768 arcseconds, and 1 ÷ 0.768 is only a little over 1.

questions.prompt: Star A is 100 times as luminous as star B, yet they appear equally bright. How much farther away than B is A?
hints: Equal flux means L ÷ d² is the same for both stars. If L is 100 times larger, what must happen to d²?
What number multiplied by itself gives 100?
questions.onCorrect: Equal flux needs L ÷ d² to be equal, so d grows as √L, and √100 = 10 times as far.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the luminosity factor. Flux falls as 1 ÷ d², so the distance factor is smaller: its square must equal the luminosity factor.
That squares the factor. The distance must grow as the square root of the luminosity factor, not as its square.

questions.prompt: A star has a parallax of 0.05 arcseconds, and a second star has a parallax of 0.5 arcseconds. How do their distances compare?
hints: Which star shows the larger shift, and which of the two is nearer?
By what factor does one parallax exceed the other?

acceptedIdeas: The first is ten times as far
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The first is ten times as far

choices.label: The first is ten times as far
The first is ten times nearer
The first is a hundred times as far

questions.onCorrect: The distance in parsecs is 1 ÷ p, so the first star lies at 1 ÷ 0.05 = 20 pc and the second at 1 ÷ 0.5 = 2 pc. A parallax ten times smaller puts a star ten times as far away.

misconceptions.feedback: A smaller parallax means a greater distance. The distance in parsecs is 1 ÷ p, so the star with the smaller angle lies farther away.
That squares the ratio, as the inverse-square law does for brightness. Distance is simply the reciprocal of parallax, with no square.

questions.prompt: What unit of distance is defined as the distance at which a star shows a parallax of one arcsecond?
hints: Its name joins the first syllables of the two words that define it.
The two ideas in the definition are the shift in position you measure and the tiny angle of one arcsecond.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The parsec: PARallax of one arcSECond. It equals 206,265 AU or 3.26 light-years.

questions.onCorrect: The parsec takes its name from a parallax of one arcsecond, and it equals 206,265 AU, or 3.26 light-years.

misconceptions.feedback: A light-year is also a distance, but it is defined by how far light travels in a year, and not by a parallax.

questions.prompt: Wien’s law gives the peak wavelength as 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K divided by the temperature. The Sun’s surface is at 5,772 K, about 6,000 K. Roughly where does its spectrum peak?
hints: Divide 2.9 × 10⁻³ by about 6 × 10³. What power of ten does the result carry?
One nanometre is 10⁻⁹ m. How many nanometres is the result?
questions.onCorrect: Dividing 2.9 × 10⁻³ by about 6 × 10³ gives about 5 × 10⁻⁷ m, which is 500 nm. The exact value is 502 nm, in the middle of the visible range.

misconceptions.feedback: That is ten times too long, a slip of one power of ten in the conversion to nanometres. One nanometre is 10⁻⁹ m.
That is ten times too short, also a slip of one power of ten in the conversion to nanometres.

questions.prompt: A star’s spectrum peaks at 290 nm, while the Sun’s peaks at about 500 nm. Using Wien’s law, λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K ÷ T, about what is the star’s surface temperature?
hints: Does a shorter peak wavelength mean a hotter or a cooler star?
Write 290 nm in metres and divide 2.898 × 10⁻³ by it. About what power of ten results?
questions.onCorrect: T = 2.898 × 10⁻³ ÷ 2.90 × 10⁻⁷ = 9,993 K, about 10,000 K, which is hotter than the Sun by a factor of about 1.7.

misconceptions.feedback: That makes the temperature fall with the wavelength. Wien’s law divides by T, so a shorter peak wavelength means a hotter star and not a cooler one.
That is ten times too small, a slip of one power of ten when writing 290 nm in metres. 290 nm is 2.9 × 10⁻⁷ m.

questions.prompt: A hydrogen line with laboratory wavelength 656.28 nm is observed at 662.84 nm, about 1% longer. The speed of light is 3.00 × 10⁵ km/s. Roughly how fast, and in which direction, is the star moving along the line of sight?
hints: What fraction of the laboratory wavelength is the shift, and what fraction of c does that make the speed?
Does a longer wavelength mean the source is receding or approaching?
questions.onCorrect: The shift is 6.56 nm out of 656.28 nm, about 1%, so the speed is about 1% of c, which is 3,000 km/s, and the longer wavelength means the star is receding.

misconceptions.feedback: A longer wavelength is a redshift, which comes from a receding source. An approaching source shifts its lines to shorter wavelengths.
That is ten times too fast. A shift of 1% means a speed of 1% of c.

questions.prompt: A star approaches at 150 km/s, and the speed of light is 300,000 km/s. By about what fraction does the wavelength of its 500 nm line change, and in which direction?
hints: What fraction of the speed of light is 150 km/s?
Does an approaching source stretch the waves or squeeze them?

acceptedIdeas: By about 0.05%, to a shorter wavelength
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: By about 0.05%, to a shorter wavelength

choices.label: By about 0.05%, to a shorter wavelength
By about 0.05%, to a longer wavelength
By about 5%, to a shorter wavelength

questions.onCorrect: The fractional shift equals v ÷ c = 150 ÷ 300,000 = 0.05%, and an approaching star is blueshifted, so its line moves to a shorter wavelength.

misconceptions.feedback: An approaching source squeezes the waves, which shortens the wavelength. Only a receding source stretches them.
That is a hundred times too large. The fraction is v ÷ c, which is 150 divided by 300,000.

questions.prompt: Betelgeuse looks orange-red and Rigel looks blue-white. What does the difference tell you?
hints: Which property of a glowing body sets where its spectrum peaks?
Test each explanation by asking whether it could change the colour of a nearby, bright star by a large amount.

acceptedIdeas: Betelgeuse is cooler, so its spectrum peaks at longer wavelengths
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Betelgeuse is cooler, so its spectrum peaks at longer wavelengths

choices.label: Betelgeuse is moving away faster, so its light is redshifted more
Betelgeuse is cooler, so its spectrum peaks at longer wavelengths
Betelgeuse is farther away, so its light has reddened on the way

questions.onCorrect: Colour tracks surface temperature through Wien’s law, so the orange-red star is cooler and the blue-white star hotter.

misconceptions.feedback: Stellar speeds of tens of km/s shift a line by a tiny fraction, far too little to change a star’s colour.
These are two of the brightest stars in the sky, near enough that reddening on the way is slight.

questions.prompt: A red dwarf has a surface temperature of 3,000 K, about half the Sun’s. Using Wien’s law, where does its spectrum peak?
hints: Does a cooler star peak at a longer or a shorter wavelength than the Sun?
The Sun peaks near 500 nm. What would half the temperature do to that wavelength, and where does visible light end?

acceptedIdeas: In the infrared, past red light
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: In the infrared, past red light

choices.label: In the ultraviolet, past violet light
In the infrared, past red light
In the visible range, like the Sun

questions.onCorrect: λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ ÷ 3,000 = 9.66 × 10⁻⁷ m, which is 966 nm. That is beyond the red end of visible light at about 700 nm, so the red dwarf gives out most of its light as infrared.

misconceptions.feedback: That has the direction reversed. Wien’s law divides by the temperature, so a cooler star peaks at a longer wavelength and not a shorter one.
The Sun peaks near 500 nm and visible light ends at about 700 nm. A star about half as hot peaks at about twice the Sun’s wavelength.

questions.prompt: A star has the Sun’s radius but twice the Sun’s surface temperature. How does its luminosity compare with the Sun’s?
hints: With the same radius the surface area is the same. What changes the power from each square metre?
How does the power per square metre depend on the temperature?
questions.onCorrect: L = R² × (T ÷ T☉)⁴ = 1² × 2⁴ = 16, so the star emits 16 times the Sun’s luminosity.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats luminosity as proportional to T². Each square metre radiates in proportion to T⁴.
That doubles the luminosity along with the temperature. The power per square metre goes as the fourth power of the temperature.
That is 2³. The power per square metre goes as T⁴.

questions.prompt: A red supergiant has a surface temperature of 3,600 K, about 0.6 of the Sun’s, and a radius of 760 times the Sun’s. How does its luminosity compare with the Sun’s?
hints: How many times larger is the star’s surface area than the Sun’s, and how many times smaller is the power from each square metre?
A surface 0.6 times as hot radiates about 0.6⁴ as much per square metre. Is that nearer a half or a tenth?

choices.label: Less than the Sun’s, since its surface is cooler

questions.onCorrect: The star has 760² = 577,600 times the Sun’s surface area, and its cooler surface radiates (3,600 ÷ 5,772)⁴, about 0.15, as much per square metre. Together that is about 87,000 times the Sun’s luminosity.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 760², the effect of the radius alone. The cooler surface cuts the power per square metre to about 0.15 of the Sun’s, and that factor has to be applied as well.
The cool surface does lower the power from each square metre, but the surface area is 760² = 577,600 times larger, and that effect is far greater.

questions.prompt: A white dwarf has a radius of 0.01 of the Sun’s and a surface temperature four times the Sun’s. How does its luminosity compare with the Sun’s?
hints: The radius is 0.01 of the Sun’s. By what factor is the surface area smaller?
By what factor does a surface four times as hot radiate more from each square metre?

acceptedIdeas: About a fortieth of the Sun’s
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About a fortieth of the Sun’s

choices.label: About a fortieth of the Sun’s
About a ten-thousandth of the Sun’s

questions.onCorrect: The area factor is 0.01² = 1/10,000 and the temperature factor is 4⁴ = 256, so L = 256 ÷ 10,000, about a fortieth of the Sun’s. A white dwarf is hot but dim because its tiny size outweighs its heat.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the temperature effect alone, 4⁴. The tiny radius also shrinks the surface area, and that effect has to be applied too.
That is the radius effect alone, 0.01². The hot surface also radiates far more from each square metre, which has to be applied too.

questions.prompt: Two stars have the same surface temperature, but one is far more luminous. Which property of the luminous star must be larger?
hints: Write L = 4πR²σT⁴ and hold T fixed.
With T fixed, the formula leaves luminosity depending on just one other quantity.
questions.onCorrect: Equal temperature means equal power per square metre, so more luminosity needs more surface, which means a larger radius.

misconceptions.feedback: The law L = R² × (T ÷ T☉)⁴ has no mass in it, so mass does not enter a comparison at equal temperature.
Luminosity is the total power a star radiates, and it does not depend on how far away the star is.

questions.prompt: Two stars have the same surface temperature, and one is 100 times as luminous as the other. How do their radii compare?
hints: With the temperature fixed, how much power does each square metre radiate in the two stars?
How does the total power depend on the radius when the power per square metre is the same?

acceptedIdeas: The luminous star is 10 times as large
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The luminous star is 10 times as large

choices.label: The luminous star is 100 times as large
The luminous star is 10,000 times as large
The luminous star is 10 times as large

questions.onCorrect: With T fixed, L ∝ R², so the radius grows as √100 = 10.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the luminosity ratio. With the temperature fixed, luminosity goes as R², so the radius ratio is smaller than that.
That squares the ratio. Luminosity goes as R², so the radius ratio is the square root of the luminosity ratio, not its square.

questions.prompt: A star has twice the Sun’s radius and four times its luminosity. How does its surface temperature compare with the Sun’s?
hints: How much of the extra luminosity does doubling the radius account for?
What is left over for the temperature to explain?
questions.onCorrect: Doubling the radius multiplies the surface area, and so the luminosity, by 2² = 4, which is all of the extra light. The temperature factor must therefore be 1, so T equals the Sun’s, 5,772 K.

misconceptions.feedback: That scales the temperature with the radius. Luminosity depends on R² and on T⁴ separately, so work out what the doubled radius already contributes.
That halves the temperature. Check how much of the luminosity change the radius already supplies before changing the temperature.

questions.prompt: Main-sequence lifetime scales as t ≈ 10 billion years × M⁻²·⁵, with M in solar masses. A star has 4 solar masses. About how long does it stay on the main sequence?
hints: What is 4²·⁵? Split it as 4² × √4.
How many times shorter than the Sun’s 10 billion years is the star’s life?
questions.onCorrect: 4²·⁵ = 16 × 2 = 32, so t = 10 billion ÷ 32, about 0.3 billion years. The exact value is 312.5 million years.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the Sun’s lifetime by the mass alone, as if the star burned its fuel at the Sun’s rate. A star of 4 solar masses burns its fuel much faster than that.
That makes the lifetime grow with the mass. A heavier star has more fuel but burns it far faster, so it lives for a shorter time.

questions.prompt: Main-sequence luminosity scales roughly as L ∝ M³·⁵, with M in solar masses. A star has twice the Sun’s mass. About how does its luminosity compare with the Sun’s?
hints: A power of 3.5 is a cube multiplied by a square root. What is 2³?
About what is √2, and what do you get when you multiply it by 8?
questions.onCorrect: 2³·⁵ = 2³ × √2 = 8 × 1.414 = 11.3, so the star is about 11 times as luminous as the Sun.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies 2 by 3.5. The exponent is a power, so 2 is raised to it: 2³·⁵ = 2³ × √2.
That makes luminosity proportional to mass. The exponent is 3.5, so luminosity grows much faster than the mass.

questions.prompt: Using t ≈ 10 billion years × M⁻²·⁵, about how long does a red dwarf of 0.5 solar masses stay on the main sequence?
hints: Given the negative exponent, does a star of half the Sun’s mass live longer or shorter than the Sun?
A negative power of one half is a positive power of two. About what is 2²·⁵?
questions.onCorrect: 0.5⁻²·⁵ = 2²·⁵ = 4 × 1.41, about 5.7, so t = 10 × 5.7, about 57 billion years. A red dwarf lasts more than four times the present age of the universe, 13.8 billion years.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the Sun’s lifetime by 0.5 only, as if the burn rate were the Sun’s. A star of half the mass burns far more slowly, so its life grows by more than a factor of 2.
That raises 0.5 to +2.5 instead of −2.5. The exponent is negative, which turns 0.5 into 2 and makes the lifetime longer, not shorter.

questions.prompt: A star starts life with 15 times the Sun’s mass. What does it leave behind when its fuel runs out?
hints: Compare 15 M☉ with the boundaries in the last screen, at about 10 M☉ and about 40 M☉.
Find which of the three mass ranges 15 M☉ falls in, then recall what each range leaves behind.

choices.label: A white dwarf, like the Sun

questions.onCorrect: Stars of about 10 to 40 M☉ end in a core-collapse supernova that leaves a neutron star.

misconceptions.feedback: White dwarfs come from stars below about 10 M☉, and this star is heavier, so its core collapses in a supernova.
Black holes come from stars above about 40 M☉. At 15 M☉ the core collapses but stops short of that.

questions.prompt: A star spends 10 million years on the main sequence, a thousandth of the Sun’s 10 billion. Using t ≈ 10 billion years × M⁻²·⁵, which is the best estimate of its mass in solar masses?
hints: If the lifetime is 1,000 times shorter than the Sun’s, what must M²·⁵ be?
Which mass, raised to the power 2.5, gives about 1,000? Try 10 and then 20.
questions.onCorrect: M²·⁵ must equal 1,000, and 10²·⁵ is about 316 while 20²·⁵ is about 1,800, so the mass lies between them, near 16 solar masses. A thousandfold shorter life needs only about a sixteenfold larger mass, because of the 2.5 power.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats the lifetime as inversely proportional to the mass. The lifetime falls as M²·⁵, so a thousandfold shorter life needs far less than a thousandfold more mass, and no known star is that heavy.
That divides 1,000 by 2.5, treating the power as a division. A power of 2.5 means M²·⁵ = 1,000, which a mass of 400 would exceed by a factor of about 3,000.

questions.prompt: What will the Sun become after its red-giant stage?
hints: Compare the Sun’s mass with the boundary for a supernova.
The Sun lies far below both mass boundaries on the last screen, so ask which end state needs the least mass.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: At 1 M☉ the Sun is well below the 10 M☉ boundary. It will shed its outer layers and leave a carbon-oxygen white dwarf about the size of Earth.

questions.onCorrect: At 1 M☉ the Sun is well below the 10 M☉ boundary, so it will shed its outer layers and leave a white dwarf.

misconceptions.feedback: Neutron stars come from stars of about 10 to 40 M☉, and the Sun is far lighter than that.
Black holes need still heavier stars, and the Sun is well below the mass required.

questions.prompt: The Andromeda galaxy is about 0.78 Mpc away, and 1 Mpc is 3.26 million light-years. About how long ago did the light we see from it set out?
hints: A distance in light-years is also the number of years the light has travelled. How many light-years is one megaparsec?
Andromeda is a little under one megaparsec away. Should the answer then be a little under or a little over 3.26 million years?
questions.onCorrect: 0.78 × 3.26 is about 2.5, so Andromeda is about 2.5 million light-years away and the light we see left it about 2.5 million years ago.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses 0.78 as if it were already in millions of light-years. The distance in Mpc has to be converted first, since each Mpc is 3.26 million light-years.
That is the conversion for one whole megaparsec. Andromeda is only 0.78 of a megaparsec away, so its light has travelled for less than that.

questions.prompt: With H₀ = 70 km/s per Mpc, about how fast does a galaxy 100 Mpc away recede?
hints: How much speed does each megaparsec add?
How many megaparsecs away is the galaxy?
questions.onCorrect: Hubble’s law gives v = H₀d, and the megaparsecs cancel: 70 × 100 = 7,000 km/s.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds H₀ and the distance. Hubble’s law multiplies them: each of the 100 megaparsecs adds 70 km/s.
That divides H₀ by the distance. Hubble’s law multiplies the two, since a farther galaxy recedes faster.

questions.prompt: With H₀ = 70 km/s per Mpc, a galaxy 50 Mpc away recedes at 3,500 km/s. A second galaxy recedes at 14,000 km/s, four times as fast. How far away is it?
hints: Is a faster galaxy nearer or farther, according to Hubble’s law?
If the speed is four times as great, by what factor is the distance greater?
questions.onCorrect: Speed is proportional to distance, so a galaxy moving four times as fast lies four times as far, 4 × 50 = 200 Mpc, which is also 14,000 ÷ 70.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the distance by 4, as if a faster galaxy were nearer. Speed grows in proportion to distance, so a faster galaxy is farther.
That squares the factor. Hubble’s law is a simple proportion, v = H₀d, with no square.

questions.prompt: Estimates of H₀ range from 67 to 73 km/s per Mpc, which are about 9% apart. A galaxy lies 300 Mpc away, and its recession speed is predicted from each value in turn. How do the two predicted speeds compare?
hints: Each predicted speed is H₀ times the same distance. What does multiplying both values of H₀ by 300 do to the gap between them, as a share of either?
Is a gap of 6 in about 70 large or small?

acceptedIdeas: They differ by about 9%, whatever the distance
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They differ by about 9%, whatever the distance

choices.label: They differ by about 9%, whatever the distance
They differ by about 6 km/s, the gap between the two values
They agree closely, since both values are near 70

questions.onCorrect: Both speeds are H₀ × 300 Mpc, so the percentage gap between them equals the gap between the two values of H₀, about 9%, whatever the distance. At 300 Mpc that is 6 × 300 = 1,800 km/s.

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets the distance. Each value of H₀ is multiplied by 300 Mpc, so the gap of 6 km/s per Mpc becomes 6 × 300 = 1,800 km/s.
A gap between the two values of H₀ carries into every distance or age worked out from it. For this galaxy the two speeds are 1,800 km/s apart, which is large enough to matter.

questions.prompt: A galaxy’s 500.0 nm line is observed at 510.0 nm, and a second galaxy’s 500.0 nm line is observed at 505.0 nm. Using Hubble’s law, how do their distances compare?
hints: How large is each shift as a percentage of the 500 nm laboratory wavelength?
The speed is proportional to the shift, and the distance to the speed. What does a shift twice as large mean for the distance?

acceptedIdeas: The first is twice as far
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The first is twice as far

choices.label: The first is the same distance, since both lines are shifted
The first is twice as far
The first is four times as far

questions.onCorrect: The shifts are 10 nm and 5 nm, which are 2% and 1% of the wavelength, so the first galaxy recedes twice as fast. By Hubble’s law its distance is also twice as great: 86 Mpc against 43 Mpc with H₀ = 70.

misconceptions.feedback: Both lines are shifted, but by different amounts. The shift gives the speed and the speed gives the distance, so compare the two shifts.
That squares the ratio. The shift is proportional to the speed and the speed to the distance, with no square anywhere.

questions.prompt: Every distant galaxy appears to recede from the Milky Way. What does this tell us about our position?
hints: Imagine standing on a different galaxy on the stretching grid.
Ask what an observer on a galaxy near the edge of the grid would see of the others, and compare that with what we see.

acceptedIdeas: Nothing special, since any uniform expansion looks the same from every galaxy
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Nothing special, since any uniform expansion looks the same from every galaxy

choices.label: The Milky Way is at the centre, since everything recedes from it
The Milky Way formed first, since other galaxies have moved away from it
Nothing special, since any uniform expansion looks the same from every galaxy

questions.onCorrect: In a uniform expansion every galaxy sees the others recede in proportion to distance, so none is at the centre.

misconceptions.feedback: Every dot on a stretching sheet sees the others recede from it, wherever the dot sits, so seeing recession does not show that we are at the centre.
Recession says nothing about how old a galaxy is, and a galaxy’s speed away from us does not show which one formed first.

questions.prompt: With H₀ = 70 km/s per Mpc, a galaxy 1 Mpc away recedes at 70 km/s. At that steady speed, about how long has it taken to cover the 1 Mpc? One Mpc is 3.086 × 10¹⁹ km, and one billion years is 3.156 × 10¹⁶ s.
hints: A distance divided by a speed gives a time. In powers of ten, roughly how many seconds is 3.086 × 10¹⁹ km ÷ 70 km/s?
How many of those seconds make a billion years?
questions.onCorrect: The time is 3.086 × 10¹⁹ km ÷ 70 km/s = 4.4 × 10¹⁷ s, and dividing by 3.156 × 10¹⁶ s per billion years gives about 14 billion years. The kilometres cancel, which leaves a pure time.

misconceptions.feedback: That is ten times too short. Dividing 3.086 × 10¹⁹ km by 70 km/s gives about 4.4 × 10¹⁷ s, and a billion years is about 3.2 × 10¹⁶ s, so check how many of those it takes to make up the total.
That is ten times too long, a slip of one power of ten in the conversion from seconds to years.

questions.prompt: The cosmic microwave background is a blackbody at 2.725 K. Using Wien’s law, λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K ÷ T, roughly where does its spectrum peak?
hints: Divide about 3 × 10⁻³ by about 3. What power of ten is left?
Is a wavelength of 10⁻³ m a millimetre, a micrometre or a metre?

acceptedIdeas: About 1 mm, in the microwave range
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 1 mm, in the microwave range

choices.label: About 1 µm, in the infrared range
About 1 mm, in the microwave range
About 1 m, in the radio range

misconceptions.feedback: That is a thousand times too short, a slip of three powers of ten. Check the power of ten left after dividing about 3 × 10⁻³ by about 3.
That is a thousand times too long, a slip of three powers of ten in the same division.

questions.prompt: The cosmic background was released at about 3,000 K and is now 2.725 K. By about what factor have its wavelengths been stretched since then?
hints: Peak wavelength is inversely proportional to temperature. When the temperature falls, does the wavelength grow or shrink?
The stretch factor is the ratio of the two temperatures. About how many times does 2.725 go into 3,000?
questions.onCorrect: Wavelengths stretch in the same proportion as the temperature falls: 3,000 ÷ 2.725 = 1,100.9, so the stretch is about a thousandfold.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the ratio upside down. The temperature fell, so the wavelengths grew: they were stretched and not squeezed.
That uses the earlier temperature alone. The factor is the ratio of the two temperatures, so divide by today’s temperature as well.

questions.prompt: For H₀ = 70 km/s per Mpc the expansion age 1 ÷ H₀ is about 14 billion years. If H₀ were 50 km/s per Mpc instead, what would 1 ÷ H₀ be?
hints: The age is 1 ÷ H₀. What happens to a fraction when its bottom gets smaller?
Would a slower expansion need more time or less to carry the galaxies to their present distances?
questions.onCorrect: 1 ÷ H₀ = 977.8 ÷ 50 = 19.6 billion years, longer than for H₀ = 70 because the expansion is slower.

misconceptions.feedback: A smaller H₀ means a slower expansion. Ask whether a slower expansion needs more or less time to spread the galaxies out to their present distances.
The age is 1 ÷ H₀, so it changes whenever H₀ does. A smaller H₀ gives a larger age.

questions.prompt: What kind of spectrum does the cosmic microwave background have? Answer with the one-word name for the spectrum of an ideal thermal emitter.
hints: It is the same kind of spectrum Wien’s law describes.
It is the spectrum a perfectly absorbing object gives out purely because of its temperature.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A blackbody spectrum, the closest to perfect ever measured, at 2.725 K.

questions.onCorrect: A blackbody spectrum, the closest to a perfect thermal spectrum ever measured, at 2.725 K.

misconceptions.feedback: Microwave says where the spectrum peaks. The question asks for the kind of spectrum it has.

questions.prompt: Why is 1/H₀ only an approximation to the age of the universe?
hints: What does 1/H₀ assume about each galaxy’s speed?
If every galaxy moved at one speed all along, distance divided by speed would give the exact time since it left. Ask whether that fits the real history.

acceptedIdeas: The expansion rate has changed over time, so no galaxy has held a constant speed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The expansion rate has changed over time, so no galaxy has held a constant speed

choices.label: The expansion rate has changed over time, so no galaxy has held a constant speed
The Hubble constant is not known exactly, so the formula gives only a rough age
Galaxies recede only from the Milky Way, so the formula leaves out the others

questions.onCorrect: 1/H₀ assumes each galaxy kept a constant speed, but gravity slowed the expansion early on and dark energy has since sped it up.

misconceptions.feedback: The uncertainty in H₀ matters, but even an exact value would leave 1 ÷ H₀ resting on an assumption about how each galaxy has moved.
Galaxies recede from every other galaxy too. Look at what 1/H₀ assumes about each galaxy’s speed.

questions.prompt: A car is now 100 km from your door, driving straight away from it at a steady 50 km/h, and it started from the door. A second car is also 100 km away, driving at 100 km/h. Which car left more recently?
hints: How long does each car need to cover 100 km at its own speed?
Which car needs less time, and so left more recently?

choices.label: Both left at the same time

questions.onCorrect: The time since leaving is the distance divided by the speed: 100 ÷ 100 = 1 hour for the faster car and 100 ÷ 50 = 2 hours for the slower one.

misconceptions.feedback: A slower car needs longer to cover the same 100 km. Compare the times the two cars have needed.
Equal distances do not mean equal times. The time since leaving is the distance divided by the speed, and the two speeds differ.

questions.prompt: A galaxy twice as far away has twice the speed. How does its time since leaving compare?
hints: Time is distance ÷ speed.
Write the time as a ratio for each galaxy, and see what happens when the top and the bottom both double.

acceptedIdeas: The same, as both distance and speed double
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The same, as both distance and speed double

choices.label: Half as long, since the speed is doubled
Twice as long, since the distance is doubled
The same, as both distance and speed double

questions.onCorrect: Distance and speed both double, so d ÷ v is unchanged: the time is the same for every galaxy.

misconceptions.feedback: The distance doubles, but so does the speed. Time is distance ÷ speed, so look at the ratio.
The speed doubles, but so does the distance. Time is distance ÷ speed, so look at the ratio.

questions.prompt: Why do the kilometres cancel?
hints: Write H₀ as km/s per (3.086 × 10¹⁹ km).
Look at the units on the top and the bottom of H₀ once the Mpc has been converted to kilometres.

acceptedIdeas: H₀ is in km/s per Mpc, and the Mpc is written in km.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: H₀ is in km/s per Mpc, and the Mpc is written in km.

choices.label: H₀ is in km/s per Mpc, and the Mpc is written in km.
Kilometres are such a small unit that they drop out.
They do not cancel, because the answer is a time.

questions.onCorrect: H₀ is a speed per distance, so with the distance in km the kilometres divide out and leave 1/seconds.

misconceptions.feedback: The size of a kilometre does not matter. The units divide out.
They do: km/s per km leaves 1/s, and its reciprocal is a time.

questions.prompt: Where does the cosmic microwave background arrive from?
hints: It fills space, left over from the early universe.
The background is the leftover glow of the whole young universe, so ask whether any single object could have produced it.

choices.label: Only the centre of the Milky Way
Only the direction of the Sun

questions.onCorrect: The glow fills all of space, so it arrives from every direction with almost the same strength.

misconceptions.feedback: The background is not tied to any one object in our galaxy. It fills space.
The Sun is far too local a source. The background comes from the whole early universe.

questions.prompt: Light of wavelength 1.0 µm set out when the glow was released and has been stretched by a factor of 1,101 since then. About what is its wavelength now?
hints: Does stretching make a wavelength longer or shorter?
A thousand micrometres make a millimetre. How many millimetres is 1.0 µm × 1,101?

acceptedIdeas: About 1 mm, in the microwave range
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 1 mm, in the microwave range

choices.label: About 1 nm, in the X-ray range
About 1.1 m, in the radio range
About 1 mm, in the microwave range

questions.onCorrect: 1.0 µm × 1,101 = 1,101 µm = 1.101 mm, about 1.10 mm, which lies in the microwave range.

misconceptions.feedback: That shrinks the wavelength. Stretching makes it longer, so the factor of 1,101 multiplies it.
That is a thousand times too long, a slip of three powers of ten. Check how many micrometres make a millimetre.

questions.prompt: A torch lights a circle on a wall 1 m away. How does the lit area change when the torch is 3 m from the wall?
hints: How does the circle’s width change when the distance triples?
Does an area grow with the width, the width squared, or the width cubed?
questions.onCorrect: The circle’s width triples and its area grows as the square of the width, so it becomes 3² = 9 times as large.

misconceptions.feedback: The width of the circle triples, but the area depends on the width multiplied by itself, and not on the width alone.
That cubes the distance, as for a volume. The light lands on a surface, so the area grows as the square.

questions.prompt: What does the flux measure?
hints: Flux is a power spread over an area.
Ask whether flux describes the star itself or the light arriving at one particular place.

acceptedIdeas: Power arriving on each square metre
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Power arriving on each square metre

choices.label: Power arriving on each square metre
How far the star's light has travelled
The total power a star gives out

questions.onCorrect: Flux is the share of the star's light that lands on each square metre, so it falls with distance.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the luminosity. Flux is only the share that reaches each square metre.
Flux depends on the distance, but it is not a distance.

questions.prompt: Why is the sphere's area 4πd²?
hints: Think about where the light has got to after travelling a distance d.
Picture all the light that left the star at the same moment, and the shape that it forms.

acceptedIdeas: The light has spread over a sphere of radius d.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The light has spread over a sphere of radius d.

choices.label: The light has spread over a sphere of radius d.
It is the area of a circle of radius d.
Because π is always multiplied by 4 in area formulas.

questions.onCorrect: After travelling d, the light is spread over a sphere of radius d, with area 4πd².

misconceptions.feedback: The 4 comes from the area of a sphere, not from π.
A circle of radius d has area πd². The light spreads in three dimensions, over a sphere.

questions.prompt: Which star is nearer?
hints: Distance is the reciprocal of parallax.
Try two example parallaxes and work out the distance for each.

acceptedIdeas: The one with the larger parallax
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The one with the larger parallax

choices.label: The one with the larger parallax
The one with the smaller parallax

questions.onCorrect: A larger parallax means a smaller d = 1/p, so the star is nearer.

misconceptions.feedback: A smaller parallax makes d = 1/p larger: the star is farther.
Different parallaxes give different distances.

questions.prompt: Star X is 3 times farther away than star Y and 4 times as luminous. How does X’s flux compare with Y’s?
hints: Which way does a greater distance push the flux, and by what factor when the distance triples?
Which way does a greater luminosity push the flux, and by what factor?

acceptedIdeas: A little under half of Y’s
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A little under half of Y’s

choices.label: A little under half of Y’s
About a third more than Y’s

questions.onCorrect: Flux is proportional to L ÷ d², so X’s flux is 4 ÷ 3² = 4/9 of Y’s, which is a little under half.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the distance, which divides the flux by 3² = 9. Star X is also four times as luminous, which multiplies the flux by 4.
That divides by 3 and not by 3². Flux follows the inverse square of the distance.

questions.prompt: A spectral line measures 500 nm in the laboratory and arrives from a star at 505 nm. By about how much has its wavelength grown, as a share of the original?
hints: How many nanometres did the wavelength grow?
What fraction of the original 500 nm is that growth?
questions.onCorrect: The wavelength grew by 5 nm out of 500 nm, and 5 ÷ 500 = 0.01, which is 1%.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the growth in nanometres, 5, read as a percentage. A percentage compares the growth with the original wavelength, 5 out of 500.
That is ten times too small. Write 5 out of 500 as a number out of 100.

questions.prompt: Which star has the shorter peak wavelength?
hints: Look at where T sits in Wien's law.
Try doubling T in Wien's law and see what happens to the peak wavelength.
questions.onCorrect: T is in the denominator, so a hotter star has a smaller λmax and looks bluer.

misconceptions.feedback: A cooler star has a larger λmax, so it peaks at longer wavelengths.
The peak depends on temperature, so different temperatures give different peaks.

questions.prompt: Why does a hotter star have a shorter peak wavelength?
hints: Look at where T sits in the formula.
Write Wien's law as λmax = b ÷ T and put a larger T into it.
