acceptedIdeas: Wien's law divides by T, so a larger T gives a smaller λmax.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Wien's law divides by T, so a larger T gives a smaller λmax.

choices.label: Hotter stars are smaller, so they give out shorter waves.
Hotter stars are usually closer, so their light arrives bluer.
Wien's law divides by T, so a larger T gives a smaller λmax.

questions.onCorrect: The constant is divided by T, so raising T lowers λmax.

misconceptions.feedback: Size does not enter Wien's law. Only the temperature does.
Distance does not change a star's peak wavelength. Only the temperature does.

questions.prompt: A star is approaching us. How are its spectral lines shifted?
hints: An approaching source squeezes its waves.
Squeezed waves are closer together, so ask what that does to the wavelength and so to the colour.

choices.label: They are not shifted by motion

questions.onCorrect: An approaching source squeezes its waves: its lines move towards the blue, a blueshift.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a redshift, which comes from a receding source.
Motion along the line of sight shifts the lines, even if the shift is small.

questions.prompt: A shift of 1% in a spectral line means a speed of about 3,000 km/s. A hydrogen line, 656.28 nm in the laboratory, is shifted by 1.31 nm. About how fast is the star moving along the line of sight?
hints: What fraction of 656.28 nm is a shift of 1.31 nm? Compare it with 1%.
If a 1% shift means 3,000 km/s, what does a shift a fifth as large mean?
questions.onCorrect: The shift is 1.31 ÷ 656.28 = 0.2% of the wavelength, a fifth of 1%, so the speed is a fifth of 3,000 km/s, about 600 km/s.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the speed for a shift of 1%, which would be about 6.6 nm on this line. The shift here is much smaller.
That makes the speed larger. A shift smaller than 1% means a speed smaller than 3,000 km/s.

questions.prompt: Dots A, B and C lie in a line on a rubber sheet, with B 10 cm from A and C 20 cm from A. The sheet is stretched evenly until every gap has doubled. How does the distance C moves away from A compare with the distance B moves away?
hints: How much does B’s gap grow when it doubles, and how much does C’s?
Does a longer gap gain more or less than a shorter one when both double?

acceptedIdeas: C moves twice as far as B
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: C moves twice as far as B

choices.label: C moves the same distance as B
C moves four times as far as B
C moves twice as far as B

questions.onCorrect: B’s gap grows by 10 cm and C’s by 20 cm, so C moves twice as far as B.

misconceptions.feedback: That would hold if both dots slid along together, but every gap stretches by the same factor, so longer gaps gain more.
That squares the ratio. Each gap simply doubles, so each gain is in proportion to its length.

questions.prompt: A galaxy is twice as far away as another. How do their recession speeds compare?
hints: Look at how v depends on d in v = H₀d.
Try a small distance and one twice as big, using the same H₀ for both.

acceptedIdeas: The farther one recedes twice as fast
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The farther one recedes twice as fast

choices.label: They recede at the same speed
The farther one recedes twice as fast
The farther one recedes at half the speed

questions.onCorrect: Speed is proportional to distance, so twice the distance means twice the speed.

misconceptions.feedback: Speed depends on distance in Hubble's law, so different distances give different speeds.
Speed grows with distance. A farther galaxy recedes faster.

questions.prompt: Why does the Mpc cancel?
hints: Write H₀ with its units, then multiply by d.
Divide the unit of H₀ by the unit of distance in H₀ × d and see what is left.

acceptedIdeas: H₀ is in km/s per Mpc, so multiplying by Mpc leaves km/s.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: H₀ is in km/s per Mpc, so multiplying by Mpc leaves km/s.

choices.label: Because speeds have no units, so the Mpc has to go.
H₀ is in km/s per Mpc, so multiplying by Mpc leaves km/s.
Because the Mpc is such a small unit that it drops out of it.

questions.onCorrect: km/s per Mpc times Mpc leaves km/s, which is the unit of a speed.

misconceptions.feedback: A megaparsec is a very large unit. The cancelling comes from how H₀ is written.
Speeds have units. Here the units come from H₀ itself.

questions.prompt: Observers in another galaxy look out at the rest. What do they see?
hints: Imagine standing on a different dot of the stretching grid.
On the stretching grid, ask whether the dot you stand on has any special place compared with the others.

acceptedIdeas: The same pattern: others receding, faster with distance
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The same pattern: others receding, faster with distance

choices.label: Galaxies approaching them, the reverse of our view
The same pattern: others receding, faster with distance
Galaxies standing still, with only the Milky Way moving

questions.onCorrect: On an evenly stretching grid every dot sees the same pattern, so no dot is the centre.

misconceptions.feedback: Gaps grow everywhere on the grid, so nothing stands still relative to anything.
Every gap grows, so other galaxies recede, not approach.

questions.prompt: With H₀ = 72 km/s per Mpc, about how fast does a galaxy 150 Mpc away recede? The speed of light is 300,000 km/s.
hints: How much speed does each megaparsec add?
About how many megaparsecs are there, and about how many km/s does each add? Multiply the two roughly.

acceptedIdeas: About 11,000 km/s, a few percent of light speed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 11,000 km/s, a few percent of light speed

choices.label: About 220 km/s, under 0.1% of light speed
About 110,000 km/s, over a third of light speed
About 11,000 km/s, a few percent of light speed

questions.onCorrect: Hubble’s law gives v = H₀d = 72 × 150 = 10,800 km/s, which is about 3.6% of the speed of light.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds H₀ and the distance, 72 + 150. Hubble’s law multiplies them: each of the 150 megaparsecs adds 72 km/s.
That is ten times too large, a slip of one power of ten in multiplying 72 by 150.

questions.prompt: Star A has twice the radius of star B, and the two stars have the same surface temperature. How does A’s total light output compare with B’s?
hints: Total light is the light per square metre times the surface area. What is the same for the two stars?
How does a sphere’s surface area depend on its radius?
questions.onCorrect: Each square metre shines equally, and surface area goes as the radius squared, so A gives out 2² = 4 times as much light.

misconceptions.feedback: Doubling the radius doubles the width, but a surface has two dimensions, so its area grows by more than that.
That uses volume, which grows as the cube of the radius. Light leaves through the surface and not through the volume.

questions.prompt: A star has the Sun's radius and the Sun's temperature. What is its luminosity in solar units?
hints: Put R = 1 and T = T☉ into the formula.
Both factors in the formula compare the star with the Sun, so ask what each ratio equals here.
questions.onCorrect: With R = 1 and T = T☉ both factors are 1, so L = 1 L☉: the Sun itself.

misconceptions.feedback: Both factors are 1 here. Nothing multiplies the result by four.
The Sun shines, and a star identical to it must do the same.

questions.prompt: Why does temperature count for more than radius?
hints: Compare the exponents in L = R²(T/T☉)⁴.
Try doubling R and then doubling T, and compare how much L grows each time.

acceptedIdeas: T is raised to the fourth power, and R only to the second.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: T is raised to the fourth power, and R only to the second.

choices.label: Hot stars are always bigger, so they radiate more.
Temperatures in kelvins are large numbers, so T dominates.
T is raised to the fourth power, and R only to the second.

questions.onCorrect: A fourth power grows faster than a square, so a change in T moves L more than the same change in R.

misconceptions.feedback: Hot stars are not necessarily bigger. The reason is in the exponents.
The size of the numbers is not the reason, since the formula compares each star with the Sun. The reason is in the exponents.

questions.prompt: Where on the H–R diagram are the hottest stars?
hints: Temperature runs backwards on this diagram.
Find the temperature axis first, and read which end of it is hot.
questions.onCorrect: The temperature axis runs backwards, so the hottest stars are on the left.

misconceptions.feedback: Cool stars are on the right, because the temperature axis runs backwards.
Height shows luminosity, not temperature. Look along the horizontal axis.

questions.prompt: A star has half the Sun’s radius and twice the Sun’s surface temperature. How does its luminosity compare with the Sun’s?
hints: By what factor does halving the radius change the surface area?
By what factor does doubling the temperature change the power from each square metre?
questions.onCorrect: L = 0.5² × 2⁴ = 0.25 × 16 = 4, so the star is four times as luminous as the Sun.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the radius factor alone, (1/2)² = 1/4. The hotter surface multiplies it.
That is the temperature factor alone, 2⁴. The smaller radius divides it.
The two effects would cancel only if they were equal. The temperature effect, a factor of 16, is larger than the radius effect, a factor of a quarter.

questions.prompt: A comet comes within 1 AU of the Sun at its closest and moves out to 9 AU at its farthest. How does the length of the long axis of its orbit compare with 9 AU?
hints: Where does the Sun sit on the long axis: between the two ends, or at one end?
The closest and farthest points are the two ends of the axis. Do their distances from the Sun add or subtract to give its length?
questions.onCorrect: The nearest and farthest points lie at opposite ends of the long axis with the Sun between them, so the distances add: 1 + 9 = 10 AU, which is longer than 9 AU.

misconceptions.feedback: The Sun lies between the two ends of the long axis. The farthest distance is measured from the Sun and not from the other end of the axis.
The nearest and farthest distances lie on opposite sides of the Sun, so think about whether they add or subtract.

questions.prompt: What is the eccentricity of a perfect circle?
hints: Eccentricity measures how stretched the ellipse is.
Eccentricity compares how far the Sun sits from the centre with the size of the orbit, so ask what that distance is for a circle.
questions.onCorrect: A circle is not stretched at all, so e is zero.

misconceptions.feedback: An eccentricity near 1 means a long, thin ellipse, the opposite of a circle.
A half-way value is a fairly stretched ellipse, not a circle.

questions.prompt: Why does aphelion use (1 + e)?
hints: Where is the Sun, compared with the centre of the ellipse?
The Sun sits at a focus, not at the centre, so ask how far a focus lies from the centre.

acceptedIdeas: The Sun is off-centre by a × e, so the far end is a(1 + e) away.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The Sun is off-centre by a × e, so the far end is a(1 + e) away.

choices.label: The Sun is off-centre by a × e, so the far end is a(1 + e) away.
Because aphelion is measured from the planet and not from the Sun.
Because e is always larger than 1 for a stretched orbit.

questions.onCorrect: The Sun is a × e from the centre, so the far end is that much farther than a.

misconceptions.feedback: e is between 0 and 1 for an ellipse. The 1 + e comes from the Sun's off-centre position.
Both distances are measured from the Sun. The planet is at the point being measured.

questions.prompt: Where does a planet move slowest?
hints: Where is the line from the Sun to the planet longest?
Equal areas in equal times: compare the length of arc the planet must cover when the line is long with when it is short.

acceptedIdeas: At aphelion, the farthest point from the Sun
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: At aphelion, the farthest point from the Sun

choices.label: At perihelion, the nearest point to the Sun
It moves at the same speed at every point of its orbit
At aphelion, the farthest point from the Sun

questions.onCorrect: A long line sweeps the same area with a short arc, so the planet is slowest at aphelion.

misconceptions.feedback: At perihelion the line is shortest, so the planet moves fastest.
Equal areas in equal times needs the speed to change as the distance does.

questions.prompt: A comet has a perihelion of 0.5 AU and an aphelion of 7.5 AU. Which is the best estimate of its semi-major axis?
hints: Do the nearest and farthest distances add or subtract to give the long axis?
The semi-major axis is half of which line?
questions.onCorrect: The long axis is 0.5 + 7.5 = 8 AU, and a is half of it, 4 AU.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole long axis, 0.5 + 7.5. The semi-major axis is not the whole axis.
That is the difference of the two distances. The Sun lies between the two ends of the long axis, so the distances add to give its length and do not subtract.

questions.prompt: A full cycle from one new moon to the next takes about 30 days. Full moon comes when the Moon lies opposite the Sun. About how long after new moon is that?
hints: Where is the Moon at new moon, and where is it at full moon, compared with the Sun?
What share of a full turn lies between those two positions?
questions.onCorrect: Full moon comes halfway through the cycle, when the Moon is opposite the Sun, so about half of 30 days, or 15 days, after new moon.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole cycle, ending at the next new moon. Full moon comes part of the way through it.
That is first quarter, a quarter of the way round. Full moon comes later, when the Moon is opposite the Sun.

questions.prompt: Which angle θ between Sun and Moon gives a new moon?
hints: At new moon, none of the lit half faces us.
Picture the Sun, Moon and Earth at new moon, and ask what angle the Moon makes with the Sun as seen from Earth.
questions.onCorrect: At θ = 0° the Moon is in line with the Sun and we see only its dark side.

misconceptions.feedback: At 90° half the disc is lit: a quarter phase, not new.
At 180° the Moon is opposite the Sun and fully lit: full moon.

questions.prompt: Why is more than half the disc lit when θ = 150°?
hints: What happens to the lit half as θ grows past 90°?
At 90° half the visible disc is lit, so ask what happens to the lit part we face as θ keeps growing towards 180°.

acceptedIdeas: Beyond 90° we see more of the lit half than the dark half.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Beyond 90° we see more of the lit half than the dark half.

choices.label: Beyond 90° we see more of the lit half than the dark half.
The Moon is closer to Earth then, so more of it is lit.
The Sun shines more brightly then, so more of the disc is lit.

questions.onCorrect: Past 90°, the lit half is turned more towards us than away, so more than half the disc shows.

misconceptions.feedback: Distance does not set the phase. The angle does.
The Sun's brightness does not change. What changes is how much of the lit half we face.

questions.prompt: After one synodic month, what does the Moon show?
hints: The synodic month is the time from one new moon to the next.
The synodic month is the time for the Moon to return to the same angle from the Sun, so ask what the phase depends on.
questions.onCorrect: After 29.53 days the Sun–Moon angle has gained a full turn, so the phase repeats.

misconceptions.feedback: The opposite phase comes halfway through the month, after half a turn.
The cycle repeats exactly. Each month brings the same sequence.

questions.prompt: The Moon is 3,475 km across and 384,400 km away, which makes its angular diameter about 0.52°. If it were twice as far away, how would that angular diameter change?
hints: Angular size is the diameter divided by the distance. What happens to a fraction when its bottom doubles?
Does a more distant object look larger or smaller?

acceptedIdeas: It would be about half as large
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It would be about half as large

choices.label: It would be about a quarter as large
It would be about half as large
It would be about twice as large

questions.onCorrect: Angular size is the diameter divided by the distance, so twice the distance halves it, from 0.52° to about 0.26°.

misconceptions.feedback: A quarter is the effect of doubling the distance on brightness or on gravity. Angular size is the width divided by the distance, which is not an inverse square.
A greater distance makes the Moon look smaller and not larger.

questions.prompt: A planet has Earth’s mass but twice Earth’s radius. How does its surface gravity compare with Earth’s?
hints: Surface gravity is g = GM ÷ R², and M is unchanged. Which way does a larger R move g?
By what factor does R² grow when R doubles?
questions.onCorrect: g = GM ÷ R², so doubling R divides g by 2² = 4, which makes g a quarter of Earth’s.

misconceptions.feedback: That halves g, as if gravity fell in proportion to the distance, whereas it falls with the square of the distance.
That makes g larger. A larger radius puts the surface farther from the centre, where the field is weaker.

questions.prompt: Which change weakens the gravitational force between two masses?
hints: Look at where r sits in the formula.
Compare how each change alters the product of the masses, the distance r, and the constant in the formula.
questions.onCorrect: Force grows with the masses and falls as r² grows, so more separation weakens it.

misconceptions.feedback: A heavier mass increases the product Mm, which strengthens the pull.
G is a fixed constant. We cannot change it.

questions.prompt: Why do we multiply the factors?
hints: In F = GMm/r², how are the quantities combined?
Try doubling M and then doubling m, one after the other, and track what happens to F.

acceptedIdeas: Each change scales the force, so the effects multiply.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each change scales the force, so the effects multiply.

choices.label: Because the formula adds the effect of each change.
Because force is the sum of two terms, one for each mass.
Each change scales the force, so the effects multiply.

questions.onCorrect: The force is a product and a quotient, so separate changes multiply together.

misconceptions.feedback: The formula multiplies its factors, so each change scales the whole force instead of adding to it.
F is built from a product and a quotient, not a sum.

questions.prompt: In g = GM/r², what does M stand for?
hints: Which mass cancelled when we divided by m?
After dividing by m, one mass is left in the formula, so ask which body it belongs to.

acceptedIdeas: The mass of the body doing the pulling
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The mass of the body doing the pulling

choices.label: The mass of the Sun, the biggest puller
The mass of the object that is falling
The mass of the body doing the pulling

questions.onCorrect: M belongs to the body whose gravity we are measuring, such as Earth. The falling mass has cancelled.

misconceptions.feedback: The falling mass is m, and it cancelled when we divided by it.
The Sun is just one possible pulling body. M is whichever body's gravity you are measuring.

questions.prompt: Two bodies are moved from separation r to 4r. How does the gravitational force between them change?
hints: Does the force grow or shrink as the bodies move apart?
The force goes as one over the separation squared. By what factor does the square of the separation grow when the separation becomes 4r?

acceptedIdeas: It becomes a sixteenth as strong
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It becomes a sixteenth as strong

choices.label: It becomes a quarter as strong
It becomes sixteen times as strong
It becomes a sixteenth as strong

questions.onCorrect: Force follows 1 ÷ r², so four times the separation divides the force by 4² = 16.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by 4 only, as if the force fell in proportion to the distance. It follows the inverse square of the separation.
That makes the force grow. It weakens as the bodies move apart.

questions.prompt: Earth’s surface curves away by 5 m over every 8 km of ground, and a ball falls 5 m in its first second. How fast must the ball travel along the ground to keep missing it?
hints: In one second the ball falls 5 m. How far must the ground curve away in that same second?
How far along the ground does it take for the surface to curve away by 5 m?
questions.onCorrect: The ball falls 5 m in 1 s, and the ground curves away by 5 m in 8 km, so the ball must cover 8 km each second to keep missing it.

misconceptions.feedback: That reads the drop of 5 m as a speed. A speed is a distance along the ground covered in one second.
That divides 8 by 5. Both figures of 5 m describe the same drop, so they match each other and are not divided.
That multiplies the two figures. The two drops of 5 m are equal, so they cancel and are not multiplied.

questions.prompt: A satellite moves slower than the circular speed at its height. What happens?
hints: Gravity pulls it inward faster than its path curves away.
Compare the satellite's speed with the circular speed, and ask whether gravity or the sideways motion wins when the speed is too low.
questions.onCorrect: Too slow and the pull wins: the path curves into the body instead of round it.

misconceptions.feedback: Escape needs more speed than the circular speed, not less.
A circle needs exactly the circular speed. Slower, the path bends inward.

questions.prompt: Why must r be in metres?
hints: Check the units of GM.
Take the square root of GM ÷ r and see which unit of r gives metres per second.

acceptedIdeas: GM is in m³/s², so r must be in metres as well.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: GM is in m³/s², so r must be in metres as well.

choices.label: GM is in m³/s², so r must be in metres as well.
Metres are the largest unit, so results stay accurate.
A square root only works on lengths in metres.

questions.onCorrect: The formula works in SI units. GM is in m³/s², so r must be in metres for the answer to be in m/s.

misconceptions.feedback: Metres are not the largest unit. The reason is the units of GM.
A square root works on any positive number. The units of GM are what matter.

questions.prompt: A probe moves at exactly the escape speed. What happens to it?
hints: The path opens out rather than closing.
Compare the probe's speed with the speed needed to stay in a circle and with the speed needed to leave for good.

choices.label: It circles at a fixed height

questions.onCorrect: At the escape speed the path just fails to close, so the probe never returns.

misconceptions.feedback: A circle needs the smaller circular speed.
Falling back needs a speed below the circular speed.

questions.prompt: A satellite circles Earth at 8,000 km from Earth’s centre, and a second satellite circles at 32,000 km, four times as far. How do their speeds compare?
hints: Circular speed is √(GM ÷ r). What happens to GM ÷ r when r is four times as large?
What is the square root of a quarter?

acceptedIdeas: The farther one moves half as fast
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The farther one moves half as fast

choices.label: The farther one moves a quarter as fast
The farther one moves half as fast
The farther one moves at the same speed

questions.onCorrect: Circular speed is √(GM ÷ r), so four times the distance divides GM ÷ r by 4 and the speed by √4 = 2. The farther satellite moves half as fast.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by 4, as if speed fell in proportion to the distance. Circular speed depends on the square root of the distance.
Both orbit the same planet, but the speed still depends on the distance. In v = √(GM ÷ r) the value of r is different for the two.

questions.prompt: At the June solstice the noon Sun is directly overhead on the Tropic of Cancer, 23.4° N, and at the December solstice on the Tropic of Capricorn, 23.4° S. How far does the overhead point travel in latitude between the two?
hints: On which side of the equator does each tropic lie?
To go from one tropic to the other, which line of latitude does the overhead point cross?

choices.label: None, since both tropics are 23.4° from the equator

questions.onCorrect: The two tropics lie on opposite sides of the equator, each 23.4° from it, so the overhead point covers 23.4° + 23.4° = 46.8°, twice the tilt. That is the whole range of the Sun’s declination over a year.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the distance from the equator to one tropic. The overhead point travels from one tropic to the other, so it crosses the equator and covers both distances.
Both tropics lie 23.4° from the equator, but on opposite sides of it, so they are different places. The overhead point has to cross the equator to get from one to the other.

questions.prompt: What is the Sun's declination around 21 December?
hints: In December the northern hemisphere leans away from the Sun.
Look at which hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun in December, and which side of the equator that puts the Sun on.
questions.onCorrect: −23.4°. The Sun is south of the celestial equator by the tilt in December.

misconceptions.feedback: That is June. In December the northern hemisphere leans away, so the Sun is south of the equator.
0° happens at the equinoxes in March and September, not at a solstice.

questions.prompt: Why is the Sun's declination +23.4° in June?
hints: Think about which way the tilted axis points.
The tilted axis keeps pointing the same way as Earth orbits, so ask which hemisphere it favours in June.

acceptedIdeas: The northern hemisphere leans towards the Sun.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The northern hemisphere leans towards the Sun.

choices.label: Earth is closest to the Sun then, so the Sun rises higher.
The Sun moves north through space.
The northern hemisphere leans towards the Sun.

questions.onCorrect: The axis keeps its direction while Earth orbits, so in June the north leans towards the Sun.

misconceptions.feedback: Distance does not set the declination. Earth is nearest the Sun in January.
The Sun is not moving. Earth's tilted axis makes it appear to shift north and south.

questions.prompt: Which noon Sun spreads the same beam of sunlight over more ground: London’s (51.5° N) at the June solstice, or the equator’s at an equinox?
hints: Find each Sun’s noon altitude first. At an equinox the Sun’s declination is 0°.
The lower of the two Suns spreads the beam more.

acceptedIdeas: The noon Sun in London at the June solstice
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The noon Sun in London at the June solstice

choices.label: The noon Sun at the equator at an equinox
The noon Sun in London at the June solstice
Both spread it equally, since each is the noon Sun

questions.onCorrect: London’s June Sun stands at 61.9°, while the equator’s equinox Sun is overhead at 90°, so London’s beam covers about 1.1 times its own width and the equator’s only its own width.

misconceptions.feedback: At an equinox the Sun’s declination is 0°, the same as the equator’s latitude, so the noon Sun there is directly overhead and spreads the beam over no more than its own width. London’s June Sun, at 61.9°, is lower.
A beam covers 1/sin h times its own width, and the two Suns stand at different heights, 90° at the equator and 61.9° in London, so they cannot spread it equally.

questions.prompt: Sydney lies at latitude 33.9° S. At the June solstice the Sun’s declination is +23.4°. How does the noon Sun at Sydney compare in height with the noon Sun at an equinox?
hints: On which side of the equator does the June Sun lie, and on which side is Sydney?
Does the Sun’s move away from the equator carry it nearer to Sydney’s zenith, or farther from it?

choices.label: The same, since the tilt changes only the length of the day

questions.onCorrect: In June the Sun lies 23.4° north of the celestial equator while Sydney lies south of it, so the gap grows by 23.4° and the noon Sun stands 23.4° lower, at 32.7° against 56.1° at an equinox.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the change for a place north of the Sun’s position, such as London. Sydney lies south of the equator, so ask whether a Sun that moves north comes nearer to Sydney’s zenith or farther from it.
The tilt changes the noon height as well as the day length. The Sun’s declination moves 23.4° from the equator, and the noon height follows it.

questions.prompt: Star X has 3 times the fuel of star Y and burns it 12 times as fast. How long does X’s fuel last compared with Y’s?
hints: Does more fuel make a star last longer or shorter? And a faster burn?
Lifetime is fuel divided by burn rate. What do 3 and 12 give?
questions.onCorrect: Lifetime is fuel ÷ burn rate, so X lasts 3 ÷ 12 = 1/4 as long as Y.

misconceptions.feedback: That is upside down. More fuel lengthens the life and a faster burn shortens it, so compare the size of the two effects.
That multiplies the fuel by the burn rate. Fuel lengthens the time and burn rate shortens it, so the two are divided.

questions.prompt: A star has more mass than the Sun. How does its main-sequence life compare?
hints: Compare how fast fuel and burn rate grow with mass.
Lifetime is fuel divided by burn rate, so think about what happens to a ratio when its bottom grows faster than its top.
questions.onCorrect: Burn rate grows much faster than fuel, so heavier stars live shorter lives.

misconceptions.feedback: More fuel, yes, but the burn rate grows far faster. The burn rate wins.
Burn rate depends strongly on mass, so lifetimes differ.

questions.prompt: Why is the exponent in M⁻²·⁵ negative?
hints: Divide M by M³·⁵.
Ask what a negative exponent does to a quantity as M increases.

acceptedIdeas: Fuel grows as M but burn rate as M³·⁵, so lifetime falls.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Fuel grows as M but burn rate as M³·⁵, so lifetime falls.

choices.label: Because mass is in solar units, which flips the sign.
Fuel grows as M but burn rate as M³·⁵, so lifetime falls.
Because lifetimes are small numbers in these units.

questions.onCorrect: M ÷ M³·⁵ = M⁻²·⁵: the burn rate outgrows the fuel, so the lifetime shrinks.

misconceptions.feedback: The sign has nothing to do with size. It comes from dividing M by M³·⁵.
Solar units set the scale, not the sign of the exponent.

questions.prompt: Using L ∝ M³·⁵, about how does the luminosity of a main-sequence star of 10 solar masses compare with the Sun’s?
hints: 10³·⁵ splits into 10³ × 10⁰·⁵. What is 10³?
10⁰·⁵ is √10. About how large is that?
questions.onCorrect: 10³·⁵ = 10³ × √10 = 1,000 × 3.16, about 3,200, so the star is roughly 3,000 times as luminous as the Sun.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies 10 by 3.5. The exponent is a power applied to 10: 10³·⁵ = 10³ × 10⁰·⁵.
That is 10³ and leaves out the half-power. The exponent is 3.5, so a square root of 10 is still to be applied.

questions.prompt: A camera on a fixed tripod keeps its shutter open for 3 hours while it points at the sky. The sky makes one full turn about the celestial pole in 24 hours, so each star draws an arc of a circle. How do the angles turned by a star near the pole and a star far from it compare?
hints: Think of two dots on a spinning disc, one near the centre and one near the edge. Which one turns through the larger angle in a second?
What does the whole sky do in 3 hours, and does it depend on which star you follow?

acceptedIdeas: Both turn through the same angle
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both turn through the same angle

choices.label: Both turn through the same angle
The star far from the pole turns through more
The star near the pole turns through more

questions.onCorrect: The sky turns as a single wheel, so every star moves through the same angle in the same time, here 3 hours at 15° an hour, an eighth of a full turn. The arcs differ in length only because the circles differ in size.

misconceptions.feedback: A longer arc comes from a larger circle and not from a larger angle. Ask how the angles compare when the whole sky turns together.
A star on a small circle is not turned any faster. The sky turns as one wheel, so compare the angle swept by a star near the hub with that swept by a star near the rim.

questions.prompt: A camera in Amsterdam is left pointing north with its shutter open for a few hours, and every star trail curves about one point in the sky. Which point is it?
hints: Think about what Earth’s axis points at.
The trails are arcs of circles, so ask what the centre of those circles is for the turning sky.

acceptedIdeas: The north celestial pole, a point in the sky
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The north celestial pole, a point in the sky

choices.label: The brightest star in the northern sky, Polaris
The zenith, straight above the camera
The north celestial pole, a point in the sky

questions.onCorrect: Earth’s axis points at the north celestial pole, so every trail curves about it, and from Amsterdam the pole stands well below the zenith.

misconceptions.feedback: The point the trails curve about is a point in the sky and not a star. Polaris lies within a degree of it, which is why Polaris seems hardly to move, but it is not the point itself, and it is not the brightest star in the northern sky either.
The zenith belongs to where the camera stands, and it sweeps across the stars as Earth turns. It coincides with the pole only at the North Pole itself.

questions.prompt: Why can we multiply 15° by the number of hours?
hints: What would change if the sky sped up?
Ask what has to stay the same from hour to hour for hours × 15° to give the right total.

acceptedIdeas: The turning is steady, so every hour adds the same angle.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The turning is steady, so every hour adds the same angle.

choices.label: Because stars speed up as the night goes on.
Because multiplying gives a bigger answer than adding.
The turning is steady, so every hour adds the same angle.

questions.onCorrect: Steady turning means each hour adds the same angle, so the total is rate × hours.

misconceptions.feedback: A bigger answer is not the reason. Multiplying works because the rate does not change.
The sky turns at a constant rate. A rate that kept changing would break the multiplication.

questions.prompt: A star has a declination of +90°. Where is it in the sky?
hints: Think about what +90° means for latitude on Earth.
The celestial poles are the points the sky turns about, so ask which one lies at the top of the declination scale.
questions.onCorrect: A declination of +90° is the north celestial pole itself, the point that the whole sky turns about, so a star there would not circle.

misconceptions.feedback: The celestial equator lies at declination 0°. A declination of +90° is as far north as the sky extends.
The south celestial pole lies at −90°. The plus sign places a star on the northern side of the celestial equator.

questions.prompt: A star has turned through 270° of its daily circle. The sky turns at 15° an hour, so a full 360° takes 24 hours. About how long ago was the star at its starting point?
hints: What fraction of the full 360° has the star turned through?
If a full turn takes 24 hours, how long does that fraction of a turn take?
questions.onCorrect: 270° is three quarters of a full turn, and a full turn takes 24 hours, so the star has been turning for three quarters of a day, about 18 hours. Equal fractions of the angle take equal fractions of the time.

misconceptions.feedback: Twelve hours would turn the star through only 180°, half of the circle. The star has turned through 270°, which is more than half.
That is the time left to complete the circle, the missing 90°. The question asks for the time already spent on the 270° turned.

questions.prompt: A navigator measures Polaris 41° above the horizon. Taking Polaris to be at the north celestial pole, what does this tell the navigator about the ship’s position?
hints: Which angle measured in the sky is equal to your latitude?
Polaris lies at the pole. Which of its angles can the navigator measure directly?

acceptedIdeas: The ship is at latitude about 41° N
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The ship is at latitude about 41° N

choices.label: The ship is at latitude about 41° N
The ship is at latitude about 49° N
The latitude cannot be found without knowing the time

questions.onCorrect: The altitude of the north celestial pole equals the observer’s latitude, so one measurement of Polaris gives the latitude directly, here about 41° N.

misconceptions.feedback: 49° is 90° minus the altitude, the angle from Polaris up to the zenith. The altitude of the pole equals the latitude itself, with nothing taken away.
The pole does not move through the night, because it lies on Earth’s axis, so its height needs no clock. The altitude of Polaris gives the latitude at any hour.

questions.prompt: From latitude 40° N, which of these stars never sets?
hints: How high does the north celestial pole stand at 40° N?
A star never sets if its circle about the pole is smaller than that height. How large is each star’s circle, 90° minus its declination?
questions.onCorrect: A star never sets when its circle about the pole is smaller than the pole’s height, so from 40° N the limit is a declination of 90° − 40° = 50°. The +60° star lies above that limit and the +45° star lies below it.

misconceptions.feedback: Its circle has a radius of 45° about the pole, but the pole stands only 40° high, so the lowest point of the circle falls 5° below the horizon each night.
Its circle has a radius of 70° about the pole, far more than the 40° at which the pole stands, so the star spends much of each turn below the horizon.

questions.prompt: At 15° an hour, about how long does it take the sky to turn through 135°?
hints: What fraction of the full 360° is 135°, and how long does a full turn take?
How long does the sky take to turn through a quarter turn, 90°, and through half a turn, 180°? Where does 135° sit between them?
questions.onCorrect: 135° is three eighths of a full turn, and three eighths of 24 hours is 9 hours. At a steady 15° an hour, the time is the angle divided by the rate.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats 12 hours as a full turn, as on a clock face. The sky takes 24 hours for a full turn, so 135° takes longer than that.
That is three quarters of 24 hours, which would turn the sky through 270°. The angle of 135° is only half of that.

questions.prompt: A star of declination +55° is watched from two places, one at latitude 30° N and one at latitude 60° N. From which place does it never set?
hints: How far is the star from the north celestial pole, and how high does the pole stand at each place?
At each place, does the lowest point of the star’s circle stay above the horizon?
questions.onCorrect: At 60° N the pole stands 60° high and the star circles it at 35°, so its lowest point stays 25° above the horizon. At 30° N the pole is only 30° high, so the same circle dips 5° below the horizon each night.

misconceptions.feedback: That has the effect of latitude the wrong way round. A higher latitude lifts the pole higher, which brings more stars into the group that never set.
A star’s declination is the same wherever you stand, but the limit for never setting is not. It is 90° minus the latitude, so it differs from place to place.
The star need not lie close to the pole, only closer to it than the pole is high. Compare the size of the star’s circle with the pole’s height at each place.

questions.prompt: On the equator the north celestial pole sits on the horizon. How many stars are circumpolar there?
hints: Where would the lowest point of any star’s circle fall, compared with the horizon?
A circumpolar star's whole circle must lie above the horizon, so ask where that circle would sit if the pole is on the horizon.

acceptedIdeas: None, because every star there rises and sets
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: None, because every star there rises and sets

choices.label: None, because every star there rises and sets
About half, those above the horizon now
Only the stars very near the north celestial pole

questions.onCorrect: None. On the equator the limit is 90°, and no star has a declination above that, so every star rises and sets.

misconceptions.feedback: Half of the sky is above the horizon at any one moment, but the turning sky carries each of those stars across the horizon before a full turn is over.
A star close to the pole traces a small circle, but on the equator that circle is centred on the horizon, so half of it still lies below.

questions.prompt: A navigator measures Polaris 41° above the horizon and, some days later, 56° above the horizon. Taking Polaris to be at the north celestial pole and each degree of latitude to be 111 km along the ground, roughly how far north has the ship sailed?
hints: What does each Polaris reading tell you about the ship’s position?
The ship sailed between the two positions. Which quantity gives that: either position’s distance from the equator, or the difference between them?
questions.onCorrect: Each reading is a latitude, so the ship moved from 41° N to 56° N, a change of 15°. At 111 km a degree that is about 1,665 km, which is roughly 1,700 km.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 41° of latitude turned into kilometres, the distance of the first position from the equator. The ship sailed only the difference between the two positions.
That is 56° of latitude turned into kilometres, the distance of the second position from the equator. The ship sailed only the difference between the two positions.

questions.prompt: A star has twice the Sun’s radius and 64 times its luminosity. How does its surface temperature compare with the Sun’s?
hints: How much of the factor of 64 does doubling the radius account for?
What is left over, and what number multiplied by itself four times gives it?
questions.onCorrect: The doubled radius accounts for a factor of 2² = 4, leaving 64 ÷ 4 = 16 for the temperature. Since 2⁴ = 16, the star is twice as hot as the Sun, at 11,544 K.

misconceptions.feedback: That takes a square root where a fourth root is needed. Luminosity goes as T⁴, so the temperature ratio is the fourth root of the factor left after the radius.
That is the fourth root of 64, which leaves out the radius. The radius also contributes to the luminosity.

flashcards.front: From latitude 41° N, how many degrees above the horizon is the north celestial pole?
flashcards.back: The pole's altitude equals the latitude: 41°.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The pole's altitude equals the latitude: 41°.

flashcards.front: The sky turns steadily through 15° an hour. If one star has been watched for twice as long as another, how do the angles they have turned through compare?
flashcards.back: The angle is twice as large. Steady turning means equal times give equal angles, so the angle is proportional to the time.

flashcards.front: At a northern latitude, how does the noon Sun at the December solstice compare in height with the noon Sun at an equinox?
flashcards.back: It is lower by the tilt, 23.4°. The Sun’s declination moves from 0° to −23.4°, so the gap to your latitude grows by 23.4° and the noon altitude falls by the same amount.

flashcards.front: Which stands higher at noon on an equinox: the Sun seen from 30° N or the Sun seen from 60° N?
flashcards.back: The Sun seen from 30° N. At an equinox the noon altitude is 90° minus the latitude, so it falls one degree for each degree you go north: 60° at 30° N and 30° at 60° N.

flashcards.front: Between new moon and first quarter, is the Moon a crescent or a gibbous Moon, and is less or more than half of its disc lit?
flashcards.back: A crescent, with less than half of the disc lit. The lit share reaches a half only when the Sun–Earth–Moon angle reaches 90° at first quarter, and the Moon is gibbous after that.

flashcards.front: One body is twice as wide as another and twice as far away. How do their angular sizes compare?
flashcards.back: They look the same size. Angular size is the diameter divided by the distance, so doubling both leaves the ratio unchanged, which is why the Moon can just cover the Sun.

flashcards.front: A planet orbits twice as far from the Sun as another. Is its period more or less than twice as long?
flashcards.back: More. P² = a³ makes the period grow faster than the distance: doubling a multiplies P² by 8, so P by about 2.8.

flashcards.front: At which end of its orbit does a comet move fastest, and how do the speeds at the two ends compare?
flashcards.back: At perihelion, where the line to the Sun is shortest. Equal areas in equal times make the speeds inversely proportional to the distances, so the speed at the near end exceeds the speed at the far end by the ratio of the far distance to the near distance.

flashcards.front: Two masses are moved from separation r to r/2. By what factor does the gravitational force between them change?
flashcards.back: F ∝ 1/r²; halving r multiplies F by 2² = 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: F ∝ 1/r²; halving r multiplies F by 2² = 4.

flashcards.front: Gravity at Earth’s surface is 9.82 m/s². How does the field one Earth radius above the surface compare with it?
flashcards.back: A quarter of it. One radius above the surface is twice the distance from the centre, and the field falls as 1 ÷ r², so it is divided by 4, to about 2.5 m/s².

flashcards.front: A spacecraft in a circular orbit speeds up until it escapes. By roughly what factor must it increase its speed?
flashcards.back: By about 1.4, which is √2. Escape speed is √(2GM ÷ r) and circular speed is √(GM ÷ r), so the 2 under the root gives the factor √2.

flashcards.front: A geostationary satellite orbits 42,164 km from Earth’s centre and the International Space Station 6,771 km. Which moves faster?
flashcards.back: The Space Station. Circular speed is √(GM ÷ r), so it falls as the orbit grows. The distance is about six times as great, so the speed is about 2.5 times smaller, near 3.1 km/s against 7.7 km/s.

flashcards.front: One star has half the parallax of another. How do their distances compare?
flashcards.back: It is twice as far. The distance in parsecs is 1 ÷ parallax, so halving the parallax doubles the distance.

flashcards.front: Mars is about one and a half times as far from the Sun as Earth is. Roughly what share of Earth’s sunlight does each square metre of Mars receive?
flashcards.back: A little under half, about 0.43. Flux follows 1 ÷ d², and 1.52² is about 2.3, so the share is about 1 ÷ 2.3.

flashcards.front: A star’s surface is about twice as hot as the Sun’s. How does its peak wavelength compare with the Sun’s, which is near 500 nm?
flashcards.back: It is about half as long, near 250 nm in the ultraviolet. Wien’s law divides by the temperature, so doubling T halves the peak wavelength.

flashcards.front: A galaxy’s spectral line is shifted to a wavelength 0.6% longer. About how fast is the galaxy moving as a share of the speed of light, and in which direction?
flashcards.back: About 0.6% of the speed of light, which is about 1,800 km/s, and it is receding. The fractional shift equals v ÷ c, and a shift to a longer wavelength is a redshift.

flashcards.front: A star has three times the Sun’s radius and the Sun’s surface temperature. How does its luminosity compare with the Sun’s?
flashcards.back: Nine times as large. Each square metre radiates the same, and the surface area grows as the radius squared, 3² = 9.

flashcards.front: A star has half the Sun’s surface temperature and exactly the Sun’s luminosity. Is its radius larger or smaller than the Sun’s, and by about how much?
flashcards.back: Larger, by a factor of 4. Halving T cuts the power from each square metre by 2⁴ = 16, so the area must be 16 times as large, and the radius 4 times as large.

flashcards.front: Does a star of 9 solar masses live longer or shorter than the Sun, and roughly how long does it stay on the main sequence?
flashcards.back: Much shorter, about 40 million years. It has nine times the fuel but burns it about 9³·⁵, or 2,200, times as fast, so t ≈ 10 billion years ÷ 9²·⁵ = 10 billion ÷ 243 ≈ 41 million years.

flashcards.front: A main-sequence star has 4 times the Sun’s mass. Does it shine about 4 times as brightly, or far more?
flashcards.back: Far more. L ∝ M³·⁵, so it shines about 4³·⁵ = 128 times as brightly as the Sun.

flashcards.front: With H₀ = 70 km/s per Mpc, how does the recession speed of a galaxy at 80 Mpc compare with that of a galaxy at 40 Mpc?
flashcards.back: It is twice as fast. Speed is proportional to distance, so doubling the distance doubles the speed: 5,600 km/s against 2,800 km/s.

flashcards.front: Two galaxies recede at 3,600 km/s and 7,200 km/s. How do their distances compare?
flashcards.back: The faster one is twice as far, since distance is speed divided by H₀ and H₀ is the same for both. With H₀ = 72 km/s per Mpc they lie at 50 Mpc and 100 Mpc.

flashcards.front: If the Hubble constant is smaller than first thought, does the expansion age 1 ÷ H₀ become longer or shorter?
flashcards.back: Longer. A smaller H₀ means a slower expansion, and a slower expansion needs more time to reach the present distances: 1 ÷ H₀ is 977.8 billion years ÷ H₀.

flashcards.front: A blackbody spectrum peaks at about 1 mm. Does Wien’s law give a temperature of a few kelvin, a few hundred kelvin or a few thousand kelvin?
flashcards.back: A few kelvin, about 2.9 K, since T = 2.898 × 10⁻³ ÷ 1 × 10⁻³. This matches the cosmic microwave background at 2.725 K.

A source recedes at 1,500 km/s. Using λ = λ₀(1 + v/c) with c = 3.00 × 10⁵ km/s, at what wavelength is its 400.00 nm line observed, in nm, to two decimal places?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Δλ = 400.00 × 1,500/300,000 = 2.00 nm, so the line appears at 402.00 nm.

question.prompt: At latitude 45° S on the December solstice, with Earth's tilt taken as 23.4°, find the Sun's noon altitude in degrees, to one decimal place.
With H₀ = 70 km/s per Mpc, find the recession velocity of a galaxy 150 Mpc away, in km/s.

The Moon is 22.15 days past new moon, with a synodic month of 29.53 days. Find the Sun–Earth–Moon angle, measured in the direction of the Moon's motion from new moon, in degrees, to the nearest whole number.
Jupiter has GM = 1.267 × 10¹⁷ m³/s² and mean radius 69,911 km. Find the gravitational field at that radius in m/s², to one decimal place.
A comet comes within 1 AU of the Sun and reaches 5 AU at its farthest. Find its orbital period in years, to two decimal places, using P² = a³.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The long axis is 1 + 5 = 6 AU, so a = 3 AU and P = √27 = 5.196, about 5.20 years.

question.prompt: From latitude 35° N, what is the smallest declination, in degrees, of a star that never sets?

Mars orbits the Sun with semi-major axis 1.524 AU. Using P² = a³, find its period in years, to two decimal places.
A planet has twice Earth's mass and twice Earth's radius. Its surface gravity is what multiple of Earth's?
The Moon orbits 384,400 km from Earth's centre, and Earth's GM is 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s². Treating the orbit as a circle, find the Moon's speed in km/s, to two decimal places.
A star's parallax is 0.065 arcseconds. Using 1 pc = 3.26 ly, find its distance in light-years, to the nearest whole number.
Earth's surface averages about 288 K. Using λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K / T, find its peak wavelength in micrometres, to one decimal place.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ / 288 = 1.006 × 10⁻⁵ m = 10.1 µm, in the thermal infrared.

question.prompt: A giant has 25 times the Sun's radius and twice its surface temperature. Find its luminosity in solar units.
Using t ∝ M⁻²·⁵, how many times longer does a 1 M☉ star live on the main sequence than a 3 M☉ star? Give one decimal place.
With H₀ = 70 km/s per Mpc, by how many km/s does a galaxy 300 Mpc away recede faster than one 100 Mpc away?
The background radiation is now at 2.725 K. If the universe expands so that wavelengths stretch by a further factor of 2, what will its temperature be, in kelvin, to two decimal places?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Temperature falls in proportion to the stretch: 2.725/2 = 1.3625, about 1.36 K.
